title: feat(bindings): hand-written stable C header with an ABI version symbol
description: Replace the cgo-generated `libsoroauth.h` with a committed, hand-written header, and export a `soroauth_abi_version()` symbol that callers can check before use.
why: `build.sh` ships whatever cgo generates, so the header's contents are a build artifact rather than a reviewed interface: a field reorder or a changed signature reaches consumers with nothing failing. Every other binding sits on this ABI, so an unversioned header makes a breaking change undetectable until a downstream build breaks.
criteria: A committed header is the published interface, and a test fails when the exported Go functions and the header disagree.
`soroauth_abi_version()` returns a monotonic integer, documented as incrementing on any breaking ABI change.
The header carries no cgo-internal types in its public signatures.
`bindings/c/build.sh` installs the committed header rather than the generated one.
guidance: There are 11 `//export` functions today; enumerate them from the source rather than from memory.
A test can parse the header and compare against the `//export` comments, which keeps the check hermetic.
Do not change any existing signature in this issue; this is about pinning what is already there.

title: feat(bindings): publish the Python package to PyPI with built wheels
description: A release pipeline that builds abi3 wheels for Linux and macOS on x86_64 and arm64, plus an sdist, and publishes them to PyPI with attestations on a version tag.
why: `release.yml` publishes the container image, `@soroauth/wasm` and the docs site, but nothing publishes the Python binding, so the only way to install it is to clone the repository and build the shared library by hand. The binding exists and is tested; it is simply unreachable.
criteria: Wheels are built for linux and macOS on both architectures, and an sdist that builds from source.
Publishing happens only from a version tag, and refuses to publish from any other commit.
The published wheel is installed in a clean environment and the golden vectors are replayed through it before the job succeeds.
Trusted publishing or a scoped token; no long-lived credential in the workflow.
guidance: `cibuildwheel` is the usual tool and handles the matrix; the shared library must be bundled into the wheel.
The existing wasm publish job already has the tag-guard and provenance pattern to copy.
abi3 keeps one wheel working across Python minor versions; state the floor in `pyproject.toml`.

title: feat(bindings): ship Python type stubs and py.typed
description: `.pyi` stubs for the package's public surface and a `py.typed` marker, checked by a type checker in CI.
why: `find` over `bindings/python` returns no `py.typed` and no `.pyi`, so every consumer gets `Any` for the whole API. For a library whose arguments are base64 XDR strings, hex payloads and ledger numbers, an unchecked signature is the easy way to pass the wrong one of three strings.
criteria: `py.typed` is present and included in the built distribution.
Stubs cover every public function and the exception types, with the error taxonomy typed as distinct classes.
A type checker runs in CI over the stubs and a small sample program, and fails on a mismatch.
A deliberately wrong call in the sample is shown to be rejected by the checker.
guidance: Read `soroauth/ffi.py` and `_ffi.py` to separate the public surface from the private one; only the former gets stubs.
Keep the stubs beside the module rather than in a separate stubs package, so they ship with the wheel.
Prefer precise aliases (for example `Base64Xdr = str`) so the three string kinds are not interchangeable to a reader.

title: feat(bindings): publish the Node binding to npm with a prebuild matrix
description: Publish `@soroauth/node` on a version tag with prebuilt binaries per platform, falling back to a source build when no prebuild matches.
why: `@soroauth/wasm` is published but the native Node binding is not, although it has a `prebuilds/` directory and an install script that looks for one. Today those prebuilds only ever exist on the machine that built them, so installing the package means having a Go toolchain.
criteria: Prebuilds are produced for linux and macOS on x86_64 and arm64 and attached to the published package or a release.
`npm install` in a clean container with no Go toolchain succeeds and the golden vectors replay through it.
The source-build fallback is exercised in CI, not just the prebuild path.
Publishing is tag-gated with provenance, like the wasm job.
guidance: `ci-node.yml` already uploads a prebuild artifact per platform; this is the consumer of those artifacts.
Read `scripts/install.mjs` for the resolution order before changing where prebuilds are looked up.
The macOS crash tracked in #518 affects the test harness, not the artifact; do not block this on it, but say so in the PR.

title: feat(bindings): publish the Rust crate to crates.io
description: Release the Rust binding to crates.io on a version tag, with the crate metadata, docs.rs configuration and a build that does not require a network fetch of the Go library.
why: The crate exists with a `build.rs` and tests but is not published, so `cargo add soroauth` does not work and the crate's version is not tied to the library's. docs.rs also never renders it, which is where Rust consumers look first.
criteria: Publishing is tag-gated and refuses a dirty or untagged tree.
The crate builds on docs.rs, where no Go toolchain exists, or documents and configures the feature that makes that possible.
`cargo publish --dry-run` runs in CI on every pull request that touches the crate.
The crate version and the repository tag cannot diverge; a test or the workflow enforces it.
guidance: Read `build.rs` first: whatever it does at build time is the constraint on docs.rs.
`docs.rs` metadata goes in `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`; a documented `cfg` that skips the native build is the usual answer.
Keep the vendored or prebuilt library story explicit in the README rather than implicit in `build.rs`.

title: feat(bindings): publish the JVM binding to Maven Central
description: Publish the JVM artifact with its native library bundled per platform, signed, on a version tag.
why: The JVM binding has a `pom.xml` and a `native/build.sh` but no publish path, so the only consumer is a local `mvn install`. Maven Central also requires signing and javadoc/sources jars, none of which exist yet, so this is not a one-line addition.
criteria: A signed artifact with sources and javadoc jars is published from a version tag.
Native libraries for linux and macOS on both architectures are bundled and selected at runtime.
A clean-container consumer test resolves the published artifact and replays the golden vectors.
The signing key is a CI secret and never appears in logs.
guidance: Read `native/build.sh` for the current output naming; runtime selection must match it exactly.
Central's requirements (POM metadata, signatures, javadoc) are the bulk of this work; check them before writing the workflow.
Keep the native library loading in one place so a new platform is a resource addition, not a code change.

title: feat(bindings): one cross-language conformance suite every binding runs
description: A single committed suite of cases — vectors, error cases and limit cases — that each binding executes in its own language, reporting results in one comparable format.
why: Each binding has its own tests, so each proves something slightly different and a behaviour can diverge in one language without any test disagreeing. `signertest` does this for Go `Signer` implementations; the bindings have no equivalent, which is exactly where divergence is most likely and least visible.
criteria: The case list is one committed data file, not duplicated per language.
Every binding runs the same cases and emits a common result format.
A case that one binding fails fails that binding's CI job and names the case.
Error cases are included, so an error mapped to the wrong class is a failure.
guidance: Derive the case list from the existing golden vectors rather than inventing inputs; add only the error and limit cases.
Each binding keeps its own thin runner; the shared thing is the data and the output shape.
Keep the format trivially diffable so a divergence is readable without tooling.

title: feat(bindings): guarantee no Go panic crosses an FFI boundary
description: Recover at every `//export` boundary and translate a panic into the ABI's error return, with a test that forces one.
why: A panic that unwinds out of an exported cgo function takes the host process with it. Every binding sits on these 11 functions, so a single unexpected nil or out-of-range in library code becomes a hard crash of someone's Node server or JVM rather than an error they can handle.
criteria: Every exported function recovers and maps a panic to the ABI error path.
A test deliberately induces a panic behind the boundary and asserts the process survives with an error returned.
The error says a panic occurred and carries no Go stack into the caller's data.
A test enumerates the `//export` functions and fails if one lacks the guard.
guidance: The enumeration test is what keeps this true as functions are added; write it first.
Recovering is not a licence to continue: the error must be terminal for that call, with no partial result written.
Do not log from library code; return the error and let the host decide.

title: feat(bindings): document and test the threading contract of the C ABI
description: State whether the exported functions may be called concurrently and from which threads, and prove it with a concurrent test under the race detector.
why: Consumers in Node, the JVM and Python each have their own threading model and are already calling into this ABI with no stated contract. The macOS crash in #518 is a thread-and-stack interaction, which is the kind of thing an unstated contract invites; whatever the answer is, it needs to be written down and tested rather than inferred.
criteria: The README states the contract explicitly, including any function that is not safe to call concurrently.
A concurrent test exercises the ABI from many goroutines under `-race` and passes.
Each binding's README points at the contract rather than restating it.
If a function requires serialisation, the bindings enforce it and a test proves it.
guidance: Read the exported functions for shared state before writing the contract; the contract must describe the code, not the wish.
A race-detector run is evidence for Go-side state only; say so rather than implying it covers the host side.
Keep this separate from fixing #518: this documents and tests the intended contract.

title: feat(integrations): authentication and authorization for the verification service
description: Pluggable request authentication for the HTTP service, with per-caller authorization over which operations are allowed.
why: `server/` has hardening tests but the service itself is unauthenticated, so the documented posture is to keep it on a trusted network. Anyone who exposes it gains an open oracle that will decode and report on any entry submitted to it, and there is currently no in-tree way to put a credential in front of it.
criteria: At least one built-in scheme and an interface for others, selected by configuration.
Authorization is per operation, so a caller can be allowed to verify but not to sign.
A rejected request returns no information about the submitted entry.
Tests cover a missing credential, a wrong credential and an authenticated-but-unauthorized call.
guidance: Read `hardening_test.go` first and extend its posture rather than contradicting it.
Constant-time comparison for any shared-secret scheme; a timing oracle here is a real finding.
Keep the default closed: an unconfigured service should refuse, not allow.

title: feat(integrations): request limits and backpressure for the verification service
description: Per-caller rate limits, a concurrency cap and a request body limit, with the rejections exported as metrics.
why: Decoding an authorization entry is unbounded work from the caller's point of view: a large delegate tree costs real CPU. With no limit, one client can starve the rest, and `decodepolicy`'s depth bounds protect correctness rather than availability.
criteria: Body size, request rate and in-flight concurrency are all bounded and configurable.
A rejection returns the appropriate status with a retry hint and is counted in metrics.
Limits are enforced per caller identity when one is available and per connection otherwise.
A test drives the service past each limit and asserts it stays responsive.
guidance: `internal/decodepolicy` already bounds decode depth and input size; reuse those numbers rather than inventing new ones.
Shed load before decoding, not after, or the limit does not protect the expensive part.
Add the counters to the existing metrics registry so the reference dashboard can show them.

title: feat(integrations): structured request logging with correlation IDs
description: Structured logs for every request, carrying a correlation ID that is accepted from the caller or generated, and propagated into the response and any trace.
why: Operating the service means answering which request produced a given result, and there is no way to do that today. The library deliberately does not log, which is correct, but the service is an application and needs it; the two must not be conflated.
criteria: One structured log line per request with method, route, status, duration and correlation ID.
A caller-supplied correlation ID is used when present and a generated one otherwise, and is returned in the response.
No entry contents, addresses or signatures appear in logs at the default level.
A test asserts the redaction, not just the presence of the fields.
guidance: `log/slog` is in the standard library and needs no dependency.
The redaction test is the important one: the natural implementation logs the request body.
Keep logging in `server/` only; the library's no-logging rule stands.

title: feat(integrations): graceful shutdown and readiness for the verification service
description: Separate liveness and readiness endpoints, and a shutdown that stops accepting work, drains in-flight requests within a deadline, then exits non-zero if it could not.
why: Under any orchestrator, a service without readiness gets traffic before it can serve it, and one without draining drops in-flight verifications on every deploy. For a signing-adjacent service, a dropped request is ambiguous to the caller, which is worse than a refused one.
criteria: Liveness and readiness are distinct, and readiness reports false during shutdown.
In-flight requests are drained within a configurable deadline.
Exceeding the deadline exits non-zero and logs how many requests were abandoned.
A test starts the service, holds a request open and asserts the drain behaviour.
guidance: `http.Server.Shutdown` does the draining; the work is the readiness flip and the deadline handling.
Flip readiness before closing the listener, or load balancers keep sending work.
Make the deadline configurable, since a long verification is legitimate.

title: feat(integrations): generate and test clients from the OpenAPI specification
description: Generate at least one client from the committed specification in CI and run it against the real service, failing when the specification and the implementation disagree.
why: `server/openapi.yaml` is committed and there is a `zz_generate_scrape_test.go`, so the specification is checked for drift against the handlers, but nothing proves a generated client can actually talk to the service. A specification that is structurally accurate can still be unusable.
criteria: A client is generated in CI from the committed specification, not from a hand-written copy.
The generated client exercises every documented operation against a running instance.
A deliberate mismatch between specification and handler fails the job.
The generated code is not committed, or if it is, a check proves it is current.
guidance: Read `zz_generate_scrape_test.go` to see what drift is already caught, and cover what it cannot.
One generator is enough; pick the one whose output is easiest to run in CI.
Error responses are the usual gap — include at least one failure path in the client test.

title: feat(integrations): audit log for every verification the service performs
description: An append-only audit record per request — who asked, what was decided, when, under which policy — written to a configurable sink and separate from operational logs.
why: #319 covers an audit record inside the library for signing decisions. The service makes decisions of its own, for callers who are not the operator, and an operator asked after the fact which entries were approved has no answer. These are different records with different retention needs and should not be the same stream.
criteria: One record per decision, with a stable schema and a schema version field.
The sink is configurable and a write failure is a request failure, not a silent drop.
Records identify the entry by hash rather than carrying its contents.
Tests cover the schema, the write-failure path and the absence of secrets.
guidance: Decide and document retention expectations; an audit log that grows unbounded gets deleted in a hurry.
Hash rather than store: the record must be useful without being a copy of everyone's entries.
If #319 lands first, reuse its record shape where it fits rather than inventing a second vocabulary.

title: feat(integrations): mutual TLS and certificate pinning for the gRPC service
description: mTLS for the gRPC signing and verification service, with client certificate verification and optional pinning, configured declaratively.
why: A gRPC signing service is a far more sensitive endpoint than the HTTP verifier: it holds or proxies signing authority. Transport security and client identity are the minimum for that, and the documented posture of a trusted network does not survive contact with a real deployment.
criteria: Server and client both require certificates, and an unverified client is refused before any method runs.
Pinning is available and optional, with the behaviour when a pin fails documented.
Tests cover an untrusted client, an expired certificate and a pin mismatch.
The insecure path, if kept for tests, cannot be enabled by default or by accident.
guidance: Read the existing service setup before adding credentials; the interceptor order matters.
Refuse at the transport layer; an authorization check inside a method is too late.
Make the test certificates generated at test time, never committed.

title: feat(integrations): streaming batch signing over gRPC
description: A bidirectional streaming method that accepts entries and returns signed results as they complete, with per-item errors that do not abort the stream.
why: `batch_sign.go` exists for high-throughput signing in-process, but the gRPC service exposes only unary calls, so a caller with ten thousand entries pays a round trip each. Unary calls also force all-or-nothing error handling, which is the wrong shape for a batch.
criteria: A streaming method handles a batch larger than fits comfortably in one message.
A failure on one item is reported against that item and the stream continues.
Backpressure is respected rather than buffering the whole batch in memory.
A test streams a batch containing a deliberate failure and asserts the others still complete.
guidance: Reuse `batch_sign.go` rather than reimplementing concurrency in the service.
The all-or-nothing rule in `AuthorizeAll` is deliberate; this is a different contract, so state it explicitly in the proto comments.
Bound the in-flight window or a client can still exhaust the server's memory.

title: feat(integrations): browser extension support for hardware and passkey signing
description: Let the extension complete a signature with a passkey or a connected hardware wallet, rather than only explaining what an entry does.
why: The extension explains an entry before signing, which is the useful half, but the user must then sign somewhere else — and the thing they sign elsewhere is not provably the thing the extension explained. Closing that gap is the point of having the explanation in the browser at all.
criteria: A passkey signature can be produced and the resulting entry exported.
The payload signed is shown to be the payload explained, by hash, in the UI.
A refusal or timeout at the authenticator leaves no partial entry.
Tests cover the happy path, a user refusal and a payload that changed between explain and sign.
guidance: `webauthn.go` and `secp256r1.go` already have the assertion parsing and verification primitives; reuse them through the wasm build.
The hash-match display is the security property; design it so a mismatch is impossible to miss.
Hardware wallet support may need a separate transport; scope it to passkeys if the transport is not available.

title: feat(integrations): offline-first signing in the browser with no network at all
description: A documented and tested browser flow that loads, inspects and signs with no network request after the initial page load, verified by a test that fails the run on any request.
why: Air-gapped signing is a real operational requirement, and the wasm build plus a passkey is enough to do it entirely in the page. Nothing currently proves the page makes no network call, so the claim cannot be made; an unnoticed analytics or font fetch would quietly break it.
criteria: A flow from entry to signed entry completes with the network disabled after load.
An automated test fails if any request is made after load, including fonts and source maps.
The page's assets are all local, with no CDN reference.
The documentation states what offline does and does not protect against.
guidance: Intercept at the browser automation layer and fail on any request; an assertion about counts is weaker.
`examples/browser-passkey` is the obvious starting point; check what it currently fetches.
Do not claim air-gap safety beyond the page itself: the host machine is still in scope, and the docs should say so.

title: feat(integrations): reproducible wasm builds with a published digest
description: Make the wasm artifact byte-identical across rebuilds of a tag, publish its digest, and verify a rebuild in CI the way `reproducible.yml` does for the binaries.
why: `reproducible.yml` rebuilds the released binaries and diffs them against the published checksums, but the wasm package published to npm has no equivalent. A browser artifact is the one consumers are least able to audit themselves, so it is the one that most benefits from a reproducible digest.
criteria: Two builds of the same tag produce identical bytes.
The digest is published with the release and with the npm package.
A CI job rebuilds from the tag and fails on any difference.
Any source of non-determinism found is documented and removed rather than tolerated.
guidance: `scripts/reproduce.sh` and `reproducible.yml` are the pattern; follow them rather than inventing a second mechanism.
Embedded build timestamps and paths are the usual culprits; `-trimpath` and a fixed date handle most of it.
Verify against the artifact actually published, not a locally built one.

title: feat(integrations): GitHub Action verifies a transaction envelope, not only entries
description: Extend the action to accept a full `TransactionEnvelope`, report every entry it contains, and fail on configurable conditions across the whole envelope.
why: The action verifies entries one at a time, but what a reviewer actually has in a pull request or a change record is an envelope. Splitting it by hand before running the action is both a chore and a place to drop an entry, which is the failure the action exists to prevent.
criteria: An envelope input is accepted and every entry in it is reported.
Failure conditions can be expressed over the envelope, such as any unsigned address entry.
The summary names each entry by index and address.
Tests cover an envelope with mixed credential arms, including a source-account entry.
guidance: `envelope.go` already has the extraction helpers; reuse them rather than parsing in the action.
Source-account entries are legitimately unsigned — treating them as a finding would make the action useless.
Keep the single-entry input working; this is an addition.

title: feat(integrations): Kubernetes manifests and a Helm chart for the verification service
description: Reference manifests and a chart that deploy the service with the readiness, limits, metrics and configuration the repository already provides, validated in CI.
why: The container image is published and the service has metrics, but there is no deployment reference, so every operator reconstructs probes, limits and scrape configuration from the source. That is exactly where a readiness probe gets pointed at a liveness endpoint and a deploy starts dropping requests.
criteria: Manifests and a chart deploy the published image and pass a dry-run validation in CI.
Probes, resource requests and metric scraping are configured and match what the service exposes.
Secrets are referenced, never inlined, and the chart fails rather than defaulting to an insecure configuration.
A smoke test deploys into a throwaway cluster and verifies one request end to end.
guidance: `kind` is enough for the smoke test and runs in Actions.
Keep the chart thin; a reference that is hard to read is not a reference.
Point the probes at the endpoints that actually exist today rather than ones this issue hopes for.

title: feat(integrations): Terraform module for the verification service
description: A module that provisions the service on one cloud, with its network posture, secrets wiring and metrics scraping, validated by a plan in CI.
why: The service is explicitly documented as needing a trusted network, which is an infrastructure property that no amount of application code can establish. Shipping the network posture as code is the only way that advice becomes checkable rather than aspirational.
criteria: The module provisions the service and its network restrictions on one named cloud.
`terraform validate` and a plan run in CI on every change to the module.
No credential is stored in the module or its state examples.
The README states exactly what the module does and does not protect.
guidance: One cloud done well beats three done partially; say in the README which one and why.
Default to private networking; a module that defaults to a public endpoint undoes the point.
A plan in CI needs no credentials if the provider is configured for validation only.

title: feat(integrations): signed SBOM for every published artifact
description: Generate an SBOM for each released artifact — binaries, container image, wasm package and each language binding — sign it, and attach it to the release.
why: The release already produces SLSA provenance and signed artifacts, which says who built them, but not what is inside them. For a signing library whose consumers have their own supply-chain review to pass, a component inventory is usually the thing they are required to collect.
criteria: An SBOM accompanies every published artifact, not only the Go binaries.
Each SBOM is signed and verifiable with the documented command.
A CI job verifies the signature and the SBOM's completeness before the release is marked ready.
The documentation shows a consumer how to verify one.
guidance: The bindings are the interesting part: each pulls in a different ecosystem's dependencies.
Reuse the existing cosign setup rather than introducing a second signing mechanism.
A generated SBOM nobody can verify is paperwork; the verification job is the point.

title: feat(integrations): continuous vulnerability scanning of the published surface
description: A scheduled job that scans the published container image and every published package for known vulnerabilities and opens an issue on a finding.
why: `security.yml` and dependency review cover the source at pull-request time, but a vulnerability disclosed after a release affects artifacts already in use and nothing is watching those. The gap between a CVE being published and anyone here noticing is currently unbounded.
criteria: The published image and packages are scanned on a schedule, not only at build time.
A finding opens an issue with the affected artifact, version and advisory.
A finding below a configured severity is recorded without opening an issue.
The job cannot fail silently: a scanner error is itself reported.
guidance: `fuzz.yml` already files issues from a scheduled run; copy that mechanism.
Deduplicate against existing open issues or a long-lived CVE reopens weekly.
Scan what was published, resolved by digest, not what a fresh build would produce.

title: feat(integrations): expose the risk analyzer through the verification service
description: An endpoint that returns the analyzer's findings for a submitted entry, with severities, in the service's documented response shape.
why: `risk.go` is the most useful thing to run against an entry you did not build, and it is currently reachable only from Go or the CLI. A reviewer with an entry and a browser has no way to get its findings, which is the situation the service exists to serve.
criteria: Findings are returned with severity and a stable identifier per finding type.
The OpenAPI specification is updated and the drift check passes.
The endpoint is covered by the same limits and authentication as the rest of the service.
The response documents that findings are heuristics, matching the analyzer's own documented limits.
guidance: Read `risk.go` for the finding types and keep the identifiers stable; consumers will match on them.
`docs/` already states the analyzer's limits — link to it rather than restating it in the API docs.
Do not let the endpoint imply approval: a clean result is not a safety guarantee, and the shape should say so.

title: feat(integrations): WASI build of the signing core for sandboxed hosts
description: A WASI target alongside the browser wasm build, so the core can run in a sandboxed runtime with no JavaScript host.
why: The browser build assumes a JS host for everything, including moving bytes across the boundary. Sandboxed server-side runtimes are a natural fit for a signing core precisely because the sandbox is a real boundary, and that deployment is impossible today.
criteria: A WASI artifact is produced and runs under at least one named runtime.
The golden vectors replay through the WASI build byte for byte.
The artifact's size is reported and budgeted like the browser build.
The documentation states which host capabilities it needs, and that it needs no network.
guidance: Read `cmd/soroauthwasm` for the existing boundary before designing a second one.
Keep the two targets sharing one core; a divergent second implementation is the thing to avoid.
`ci-wasm.yml` already enforces a size budget — extend it rather than adding a parallel check.

title: feat(integrations): fixture contract exercising every credential arm in one transaction
description: A contract and e2e scenario that requires authorization from a source-account entry, a legacy address entry, a V2 entry and a delegates entry in a single transaction.
why: The e2e scenarios each prove one arm. Nothing proves the arms compose, and the host checks them together: an entry ordering or nonce interaction that only appears when all four are present would pass every test in the repository today.
criteria: One transaction carries all four credential arms and is accepted on testnet.
The scenario logs the hash, the ledger and the arm observed for each submitted entry, decoded from the envelope.
A negative variant with one arm's signature removed is rejected, and the raw error is reported.
`RESULTS.md` records the run.
guidance: Reuse the shared fixture deployment harness rather than deploying another contract from scratch.
Two simulation passes are required once delegates are involved; the existing delegate scenario shows the shape.
Decode the submitted envelope to report the arms, as the existing scenarios do; do not assume what was sent.

title: feat(integrations): replay a recorded RPC flow against a live network to detect drift
description: A scheduled job that replays the recorded RPC fixtures against live testnet and reports where the real responses no longer match the recordings.
why: `rpcflow/rpcfixture` makes the offline flow tests fast and hermetic, which is right, but it also means those tests keep passing after the network's responses change shape. The fixtures' value depends on someone noticing when they go stale, and nothing does.
criteria: A scheduled job replays each fixture against testnet and reports differences.
A difference opens an issue naming the fixture and the field that moved.
The job distinguishes a changed response shape from a transient network failure.
Pull-request runs stay offline and are unaffected.
guidance: Compare shapes and the fields the tests rely on, not whole payloads, or ledger numbers make every run differ.
Reuse the issue-filing pattern from `fuzz.yml`.
Never let this job rewrite the fixtures automatically; a human should see the diff.

title: feat(integrations): Stellar Wallets Kit adapter conformance against a real wallet
description: Drive the wallet adapter through a real wallet implementation in a browser automation test, covering connect, sign and refuse.
why: `adapters/walletsdk` is unit-tested against the interface it expects, which proves it is self-consistent rather than that it works with any real wallet. The adapter's whole purpose is the integration, and that is the part with no coverage.
criteria: A browser test drives connect, sign and user-refusal paths against a real wallet build.
The signed entry produced is byte-compared against a golden vector.
A refusal leaves no partial entry and surfaces a typed error.
The test runs in CI, or is scheduled with its skip reason reported when it cannot.
guidance: A mock that implements the same interface proves nothing new; this needs the real implementation.
If the wallet cannot run headless in CI, say so plainly and schedule the job rather than pretending it runs per pull request.
Pin the wallet version; an unpinned dependency makes this test a source of random failures.

title: feat(signers): distributed key generation for the threshold signer
description: A DKG ceremony that produces FROST key shares without any participant ever holding the full private key, with a verifiable transcript.
why: `frost.go` can sign with real key shares, but the shares have to come from somewhere, and today that means generating a key and splitting it — a moment when one machine holds everything. That single point of compromise defeats the reason for threshold signing in the first place.
criteria: Shares are produced with no participant and no coordinator ever holding the full key.
Each participant can verify the ceremony completed correctly and that its share matches the group key.
A participant that aborts or sends a malformed contribution is identified and the ceremony fails closed.
Tests cover the happy path, an aborting participant and a malformed contribution.
guidance: Read `frost/frost.go` for the share representation already in use; the DKG must produce exactly that.
Fail closed: a ceremony that cannot be verified must produce no usable share.
Cite the FROST specification section for each check rather than describing the maths from memory.

title: feat(signers): refresh threshold shares without changing the group key
description: Proactive resharing that gives every participant a new share for the same public key, so an attacker must compromise a threshold within one refresh window.
why: Without refresh, shares are valid for the lifetime of the account, and an attacker who takes one share per year eventually has a threshold. The account address cannot change, so re-keying is not an option and resharing is the only answer.
criteria: After a refresh the group public key and the account address are unchanged.
Old shares cannot be combined with new ones to sign.
A participant that misses a refresh is detected and cannot silently keep signing with a stale share.
A test signs before and after a refresh and proves the mixed-share case fails.
guidance: The mixed-share rejection is the property that matters most; write that test first.
Depends on the DKG work for its transcript machinery — say so in the issue rather than duplicating it.
Document the operational procedure, not just the API: a refresh nobody can run is not a mitigation.

title: feat(signers): identifiable abort for a failed threshold signing round
description: When a threshold round fails, report which participant produced the invalid contribution, with evidence another party can check.
why: A round that fails with 'signing failed' is operationally useless: with five participants the operator cannot tell a broken machine from a malicious one, and the only recovery is to retry and hope. Attribution is what turns a failure into an action.
criteria: A failed round names the participant whose contribution was invalid.
The accusation carries evidence that a third party can verify independently.
A participant cannot frame another by sending a crafted contribution, and a test proves it.
The error type is distinct from a transport or timeout failure.
guidance: Distinguish unavailable from invalid: a timeout is not an accusation and must not be reported as one.
The anti-framing test is the hard part and the reason this is not a logging change.
Keep the evidence small enough to include in an audit record.

title: feat(signers): signed transcript for every threshold signing session
description: A record of each session — participants, payload, rounds, outcome — signed by the coordinator so it can be audited after the fact.
why: Multi-party signing is used precisely where someone will later ask who authorized what. `coordinator.go` orchestrates the rounds but keeps no durable account of them, so that question has no answer and the audit property people adopt threshold signing for is missing.
criteria: Every session produces a transcript identifying participants, the payload hash and the outcome.
The transcript is signed and verifiable without the coordinator's cooperation.
A failed or aborted session produces a transcript too, with its failure reason.
No key share or private material appears in a transcript, asserted by a test.
guidance: Hash the payload rather than storing it; the transcript should not become a copy of every entry.
Reuse the audit record shape from #319 if it has landed, rather than inventing a second vocabulary.
A transcript only the coordinator can verify is worthless — independent verification is the requirement.

title: feat(signers): authenticated transport for coordinator rounds
description: Mutual authentication and replay protection between the coordinator and participants, so a round's messages cannot be injected, replayed or reordered by the network.
why: `coordinator.go` defines the rounds but leaves the channel to the caller, which means the security of a multi-party signature currently rests on undocumented assumptions about someone else's transport. An attacker who can inject a round message can influence which payload gets signed.
criteria: Participants and coordinator authenticate each other before any round material is exchanged.
Replayed and reordered messages are rejected, and a test proves both.
Session binding prevents a message from one session being accepted in another.
The documentation states the transport's requirements for anyone supplying their own.
guidance: Bind every message to a session identifier and a round number; that is what stops cross-session replay.
Do not invent a handshake if an existing authenticated channel can be required instead — but then document that requirement loudly.
The cross-session replay test is the one most likely to find a real bug.

title: feat(signers): asynchronous approval signer for human-in-the-loop custody
description: A signer whose `Sign` can return a pending state, with a handle to resume when an out-of-band approval completes, rather than blocking a request for minutes.
why: Fireblocks, Turnkey and any policy desk may take minutes or hours to approve. The `Signer` contract is synchronous, so the only options today are to block a goroutine for an hour or to lose the request; neither is viable in a server handling other traffic.
criteria: A pending result carries a durable handle that survives process restart.
Resuming with a handle returns the signature or a terminal rejection, and never a silently different payload.
The payload is bound to the handle so an approval cannot be redirected to another entry, proved by a test.
The existing synchronous `Signer` contract is unchanged for signers that do not need this.
guidance: The payload binding is the security property: an approval for entry A must be unusable for entry B.
Do not change the `Signer` interface; add a capability a signer can also implement, which `signer_cache.go` and `hooks.go` already suggest as a pattern.
State the durability requirement on the handle store rather than assuming a database.

title: feat(signers): circuit breaker and health checking for remote signers
description: Track a remote signer's recent failures, open a breaker when it is unhealthy, and report health so a chain can route around it before a request fails.
why: #330-era retry and backoff makes one call more likely to succeed; it does nothing about a signer that is simply down, where every request pays the full retry budget before failing. `chain.go` has fallback but no notion of health, so it only learns a signer is dead by failing on it each time.
criteria: A breaker opens after a configured failure pattern and short-circuits subsequent calls.
Health is observable, and `chain.go` can prefer a healthy signer.
A half-open probe recovers automatically when the signer returns.
A breaker never converts a refusal-to-sign into a retryable failure, asserted by a test.
guidance: Distinguish a transport failure from a deliberate refusal; conflating them would retry a policy decision.
Read `chain.go` for the existing fallback and quorum semantics before adding routing.
Keep the breaker's state per signer identity, not per process-wide signer type.

title: feat(signers): per-signer observability through the hooks interface
description: Emit latency, outcome and retry counts per signer identity through the existing hooks, with a reference dashboard panel.
why: `hooks.go` provides metrics and tracing hooks for the library's operations, but a deployment with a KMS signer, a passkey signer and a remote signer cannot tell which one is slow or failing. That is the first question during an incident and it currently has no instrumentation.
criteria: Latency and outcome are recorded per signer identity, not aggregated across signers.
Retry and breaker events are distinguishable from first-attempt failures.
No address, payload or signature is used as a metric label.
The reference dashboard gains a panel and a test asserts the metric names are stable.
guidance: Unbounded label values are the classic mistake here: addresses must never become labels.
Extend the existing hooks rather than adding a second instrumentation path.
The name-stability test is what keeps dashboards from breaking silently.

title: feat(signers): verify a KMS key is non-exportable before trusting it
description: Query each KMS for the key's origin and exportability at construction time and refuse, or warn loudly, when the key material could have left the HSM.
why: The reason to use a KMS signer is that the key never leaves the service, but both adapters accept any key identifier, including an imported key whose material exists elsewhere. The adapter therefore cannot deliver the property it is chosen for, and the caller has no way to tell.
criteria: Construction checks the key's origin and protection level through the provider's API.
A key that does not meet the configured requirement is refused by default.
The requirement can be relaxed explicitly, and doing so is recorded.
Tests cover an HSM-backed key, an imported key and a key whose metadata cannot be read.
guidance: Read each provider's field names from their API documentation and cite them; do not guess.
Fail closed: unknown metadata should be refused rather than assumed acceptable.
One extra call at construction is acceptable; do not add one per signature.

title: feat(signers): enforce user verification and credential backup policy for passkeys
description: Let a caller require user verification and reject or flag synced, backup-eligible credentials, enforced when an assertion is parsed.
why: `webauthn.go` parses assertions, but the UV, BE and BS flags carry the difference between a hardware-bound credential and one synced through a consumer cloud account. For an account that moves money, that distinction is the whole security model, and nothing enforces it today.
criteria: A policy can require user verification and an assertion without it is refused.
Backup-eligible and backed-up credentials are distinguishable and can be refused.
The default is documented explicitly rather than implied.
Tests cover each flag combination, including a UV-absent assertion.
guidance: Read the flag semantics from the WebAuthn specification and cite the section; BE and BS are easy to invert.
Enforce at parse time so no caller can accidentally skip the check.
State the trade-off in the docs: requiring hardware-bound credentials loses account recovery.

title: feat(signers): authenticator model allowlist from FIDO metadata
description: Verify an enrolling authenticator's AAGUID against FIDO Metadata Service data, so an account can require specific certified models.
why: #331-era attestation verification proves an attestation statement is well formed and signed, not that the authenticator is a model anyone trusts. Without metadata, a self-signed software authenticator and a certified hardware key are indistinguishable at enrolment, which is when the decision matters.
criteria: An AAGUID is checked against a pinned metadata snapshot, not fetched live during enrolment.
An allowlist and a denylist are both expressible, and an unknown AAGUID has a documented default.
The snapshot's provenance and date are recorded, and a stale snapshot is reported.
Tests cover an allowed model, a denied model and an unknown AAGUID.
guidance: Pin a snapshot and commit its digest; fetching metadata during enrolment makes enrolment depend on a third party being up.
Default to refusing unknown models for the strict policy and say so, rather than quietly allowing.
Do not vendor the whole metadata blob if a digest and a fetch step will do; keep the repository small.

title: feat(signers): assert no signer error or string carries key material
description: A conformance dimension that drives every signer through its failure paths and asserts no error, `String` method or formatted value contains private material.
why: There are now a dozen signers across hardware, cloud and remote transports, and each formats its own errors. A wrapped provider error that happens to include a key handle, a share or a seed would reach a log, and nothing checks for it; the pattern is common enough that it needs a test rather than review.
criteria: Every signer in the repository runs the check as part of the conformance suite.
Failure paths are exercised, not only the happy path.
The check covers errors, `String`/`Format` output and any struct printed with `%v`.
A deliberately leaky test signer is shown to fail the check.
guidance: The deliberately leaky signer is what proves the test bites; include it as a fixture and show the failure in the pull request.
Seed the check with recognisable sentinel key material so a match is unambiguous.
`signertest` already enumerates signers for conformance — extend it rather than writing a separate audit.

title: feat(signers): batch ed25519 verification for large signature sets
description: Verify many ed25519 signatures together rather than one at a time, where the batch API is faster, behind an identical-result guarantee.
why: `batch.go` and the verification engine check signatures in a loop, which dominates the cost of verifying thousands of entries. Batch verification is substantially faster, but it has different failure semantics — a batch fails as a whole — so it needs a careful API rather than a drop-in swap.
criteria: A batch path exists and is measurably faster, with a committed benchmark showing the crossover point.
A batch containing one bad signature identifies which one, by falling back rather than failing opaquely.
Results are identical to the per-signature path for every golden vector.
The per-signature path remains the default unless the caller opts in.
guidance: The identical-results property is non-negotiable; a differential test against the existing path is the way to prove it.
Report the crossover honestly: below some batch size this is slower, and the benchmark should say so.
Do not weaken verification to gain speed; a batch that cannot attribute a failure must fall back.

title: feat(signers): allocate a timeout budget across a delegate tree
description: Given one deadline for signing a whole tree, divide it across the nodes to be signed so a slow signer cannot consume the entire budget.
why: Every signing call takes a context, and the deadline is passed down unchanged, so the first slow signer in a ten-delegate tree can exhaust the deadline and leave the rest unattempted. The caller then sees a timeout without knowing the tree was only partly tried.
criteria: A whole-tree deadline is divided across nodes, with the policy documented.
Exhausting the budget reports which nodes were not attempted.
No partial entry is returned on a timeout, consistent with the existing no-partial-result rule.
Tests cover one slow signer, all signers slow, and a deadline already expired on entry.
guidance: Read `planner.go` for the existing traversal order before imposing a budget on it.
The no-partial-result rule is a hard constraint — a timeout must leave the caller's entry untouched.
Equal division is a fine first policy; document it as a choice rather than presenting it as optimal.

title: feat(signers): air-gapped signing exchange over files
description: A documented file format and commands to carry a signing request to an offline machine and bring the signature back, with the payload bound into both files.
why: The strongest custody story is a machine that has never been on a network, and it is unreachable today: every signer assumes a live transport. A file exchange is the only mechanism that works across an air gap, and inventing it ad hoc per operator is how payload-substitution mistakes happen.
criteria: A request file carries everything an offline signer needs, including the full preimage.
A response file is bound to the request, so a signature cannot be applied to a different entry.
The offline side needs no network and no state from the online side beyond the file.
Tests cover a mismatched response, a truncated file and a response reused against another request.
guidance: Bind by payload hash and check it on the way back in; that single check prevents the main attack.
Reuse the `remote/protocol.go` message shapes where they fit rather than designing a third format.
Keep the format readable enough that an operator can inspect it before signing.

title: feat(signers): construct any signer from a configuration URI
description: Build a signer from a single string such as `awskms://...` or `vault://...`, with a registry so adapters can register their own scheme.
why: A service that needs to switch custody backends by configuration currently has to compile in every adapter and write a selection switch. That is the main reason the adapters sit unused in deployments that would otherwise benefit from them.
criteria: A URI selects and configures a signer, with a registry for out-of-tree schemes.
No secret is ever accepted inside the URI, and a URI containing one is refused.
An unknown scheme fails with a message listing the registered ones.
Tests cover every in-tree scheme and a URI carrying a secret.
guidance: Refusing secrets in the URI is the important rule: URIs end up in logs, process lists and crash reports.
Adapters are separate modules, so registration must be explicit rather than by import side effect from the root package.
Mirror the CLI's existing `--secret-env` discipline: name the variable, never the value.

title: feat(api): persistence interface for the nonce tracker
description: An interface behind the nonce tracker plus at least one durable implementation, so tracked nonces survive a restart.
why: `noncetracker.go` prevents nonce reuse within a process. A restart loses that memory, which is exactly when a retry loop replays a stored entry, and the host's rejection then arrives after fees are spent. The guard is only as good as its durability.
criteria: The tracker works behind an interface and the in-memory implementation remains the default.
At least one durable implementation is provided and tested.
Concurrent use is safe and covered under `-race`.
A test proves a nonce recorded before a simulated restart is still refused afterwards.
guidance: Read `noncetracker.go` for the current semantics; the interface must not quietly change them.
Expiry matters: a store that never forgets grows without bound, so document the retention rule.
Keep durable backends dependency-light, or put them in their own module as the adapters are.

title: feat(api): preflight an entry against a network's configured limits
description: Given a network's current settings, report whether an entry would be rejected for an expiration beyond `max_live_until_ledger` or for exceeding a protocol limit, before it is submitted.
why: The expiration semantics are documented as deliberately not hard-coding a cap, because the library cannot know the network's setting offline. That is right, but it leaves every caller to discover the limit by having a transaction rejected after paying fees.
criteria: Given the network settings, an entry is reported as acceptable or not, with the reason.
The settings are an input, never fetched or assumed by the library.
The inclusive expiration boundary matches the host's documented behaviour exactly.
Tests cover an expiration at, one below and one above the limit.
guidance: The boundary is inclusive: the host rejects only when the current ledger is past the expiration. Cite the host source.
Keep this pure; `rpcflow` is where fetching settings belongs if anyone wants that.
Do not reintroduce a hard-coded cap, even as a default.

title: feat(api): report which protocol version an entry requires
description: For a given entry, report the minimum protocol version that can process it, derived from its credential arm and invocation types.
why: `protocolmatrix.go` holds the compatibility information, but a caller holding an entry cannot ask the direct question: will this network accept it? Submitting a CAP-71 entry to a network that predates it fails in a way that is hard to read, and the answer is computable offline.
criteria: Every credential arm and invocation function type maps to a minimum version.
The answer is derived from the entry, including nested delegates, not from a caller hint.
An unknown arm or function type is an error rather than an optimistic answer.
A test covers each arm and asserts the matrix and this function cannot disagree.
guidance: Read `protocolmatrix.go` and reuse its data; a second copy of the mapping is the failure to avoid.
Fail closed on unknown inputs: guessing a version here produces a confident wrong answer.
The consistency test between the matrix and this function is what keeps it true.

title: feat(api): wall-clock estimates for expiration ledgers
description: Convert between a ledger number and an approximate time, so an expiration can be expressed and reported in human terms with its uncertainty.
why: `ExpirationAfter` counts ledgers, but every operator reasons in minutes and hours, and the conversion gets done approximately in someone's head or hard-coded at five seconds per ledger. Ledger time varies, so an estimate presented without error bounds is how signatures end up expiring earlier than intended.
criteria: Conversion works in both directions and returns an interval rather than a single time.
The assumed ledger rate is an explicit input with a documented default and source.
The uncertainty is part of the result and is carried into any formatted output.
Tests cover a rate change and assert the interval widens with distance.
guidance: Return a range, not a point: a false-precision timestamp here is actively harmful.
Read `ledger.go` for anything that already assumes a rate and make it consistent.
Cite the source for the default rate rather than stating it from memory.

title: feat(api): stable fingerprint for an authorization entry
description: A short, stable identifier for an entry that is independent of its signatures, so the same authorization can be tracked across signing stages.
why: `Equal` compares whole encoded entries, so an entry before and after signing compares unequal although it authorizes the same thing. Logs, audit records and the diff tooling all need a way to say 'this is the same authorization, further along', and each currently invents one.
criteria: The fingerprint is unchanged by adding or changing signatures and by the expiration write.
It changes whenever anything that is signed changes.
It is stable across library versions, with a versioned prefix so a future change is visible.
Property tests assert both directions of the invariant over generated entries.
guidance: `canonical.go` already defines a canonical form — build on it rather than defining a second notion of sameness.
The precise boundary of what the fingerprint ignores must match what the preimage ignores; derive it from `preimage.go`.
Version the output format from the start; an unversioned identifier can never be changed.

title: feat(api): redact an entry for logs and support bundles
description: Produce a reduced form of an entry that keeps its structure for diagnosis while removing signatures and optionally addresses, with the redaction stated in the output.
why: Debugging a failed authorization means sending someone an entry, and an entry contains signatures and account addresses. People paste the whole base64 into issues today because there is no supported alternative, and the documentation's advice to be careful with hostile entries does not help the person sharing their own.
criteria: The redacted form keeps the tree shape, arms and counts needed to diagnose a problem.
Signatures are always removed and addresses are removable, with the choices recorded in the output.
The redacted form is explicitly not re-signable and cannot be mistaken for an entry.
A test asserts no signature bytes survive any redaction level.
guidance: Make the output obviously not an entry — a different encoding — so nobody tries to submit one.
Reuse `Inspect`'s report rather than designing a third description of an entry.
State in the docs that a redacted entry can still identify an account if addresses are kept.

title: feat(api): cost model for a delegate plan
description: Estimate the signing work, signature count and resource-fee impact of a delegate plan before committing to it, so two plans can be compared.
why: `planner.go` builds delegate trees and #306 computes the fee delta signatures add, but nothing lets a caller compare two candidate plans. A tree that authorizes the same thing can differ several-fold in signatures and fee, and that choice is currently made blind.
criteria: A plan yields a comparable estimate without performing any signing.
The estimate covers signature count, signing round trips and fee impact.
Two plans for the same authorization are comparable and the cheaper one is identifiable.
The estimate's accuracy is checked against a real signed entry in a test.
guidance: Build on #306's fee work if it has landed rather than reimplementing the fee delta.
Report estimates as estimates, with the assumptions listed; precision here would be false.
The accuracy test against a real entry is what keeps the model honest.

title: feat(api): typed traversal of an invocation's ScVal arguments
description: A typed walk over an invocation's arguments, so a caller can find the addresses and amounts inside them without hand-decoding XDR unions.
why: The security question about an entry is almost always inside the arguments — which address receives, what amount. `Inspect` reports the function and an argument count, so anyone asking the real question drops into `go-stellar-sdk`'s unions and writes the traversal themselves, which is where the mistakes are.
criteria: Every `ScVal` type is handled, including nested maps and vectors, with no panic on any input.
Addresses and integer amounts anywhere in the tree can be located by a caller.
Depth and size bounds from the decode policy apply to the traversal.
A fuzz target runs the traversal over arbitrary input and finds no panic.
guidance: Enumerate the `ScVal` arms from the SDK source and cite the file; a missed arm is a panic.
Reuse `internal/decodepolicy` for the bounds instead of adding new limits.
This is reporting only — it must not influence what is signed.

title: feat(api): compare an entry against the simulation that produced it
description: Check that an entry about to be signed matches the simulation response it came from, and report any difference as a structured finding.
why: The normal flow is simulate, then sign what came back, and nothing verifies that the entry being signed is still the entry simulated. An entry altered between those steps — by a bug or a hostile intermediary — is signed without complaint, and that is the single highest-value check in the whole flow.
criteria: An entry and a simulation response are compared and differences reported per field path.
A changed invocation, address or nonce is a finding; an added signature is not.
The comparison is available before signing and is cheap enough to run every time.
Tests cover an unmodified entry and a tampered one for each arm.
guidance: `diff.go` already distinguishes payload-affecting changes from signature changes; reuse that distinction exactly.
`rpcflow/rpcfixture` has recorded responses to test against without a network.
Make it easy to call: a check nobody runs because it is awkward provides no protection.

title: feat(api): machine-readable code on every exported error
description: Give each sentinel error a stable string code, exposed through an interface, so callers and bindings can branch on it without matching message text.
why: The bindings each map Go errors to their own exception types by inspecting the error, and the CLI has machine-readable output, so the message text has effectively become an API that nothing protects. Rewording an error for clarity can silently break a binding's error mapping.
criteria: Every exported sentinel carries a stable code, and a test asserts the codes are unique.
A test fails if a sentinel is added without a code.
The bindings map on codes rather than on message text.
The codes are documented as stable, with a stated policy for changing one.
guidance: `errors.Is` stays the Go-side mechanism; codes are for crossing language boundaries.
The completeness test is what matters: enumerate sentinels and require a code for each.
Once published, a code cannot change — say so in the documentation and the policy.

title: feat(api): injectable clock and ledger source for deterministic tests
description: Let callers supply the current time and latest ledger wherever the library derives an expiration, so downstream tests are deterministic.
why: Anything computing a relative expiration reads an ambient current ledger, so a downstream test either hard-codes a number that goes stale or is time-dependent and flaky. #323's test builders will hit the same wall, and the fix belongs in the library rather than in every consumer.
criteria: Every path deriving an expiration accepts an injectable source, with the ambient one as default.
A test using a fixed source produces identical output across runs.
No new global or package-level mutable state is introduced.
The existing call signatures keep working unchanged.
guidance: Pass the source explicitly rather than through a package variable; a global here is a data race waiting to happen.
Grep for every place a current ledger or time is read before designing the interface.
Keep the default behaviour byte-identical, proved by the golden vectors.

title: feat(api): bound the total work an entry can demand
description: A total-work budget across decode, traversal and verification, so a structurally legal entry cannot cost unbounded CPU.
why: `decodepolicy` bounds decode depth and input size, which stops the obvious attacks, but a legal entry within those bounds can still have a wide delegate tree with many signatures to verify. The verification service and the browser build both process untrusted entries, and neither has a ceiling on the work one request can cause.
criteria: A single budget covers decode, traversal and signature verification.
Exceeding it returns a distinct, typed error naming the budget.
The default is documented with the measurement that justifies it.
A test uses a legal but expensive entry and asserts it is refused within the budget.
guidance: Measure before choosing the default and report the numbers; an invented limit is either useless or breaks real entries.
Extend `decodepolicy` rather than adding a parallel limit mechanism.
Keep tightening possible and loosening beyond the default impossible, as the decode limits already do.

title: feat(api): progress observation for long batch operations
description: Report progress during a long batch sign or verify, so a caller can show it and cancel knowing how far it got.
why: `batch_sign.go` handles high-throughput batches that can run for a long time. From outside, the call is opaque until it returns, so a CLI or service has nothing to display and an operator cancelling has no idea whether it was nearly done.
criteria: Progress is reported through the existing hooks, with completed and total counts.
Reporting adds no measurable cost when no observer is attached, shown by a benchmark.
Cancellation reports how far it got, without returning a partial result.
The TUI or CLI consumes it, so the feature has a real caller.
guidance: Extend `hooks.go` rather than adding a callback parameter to the batch API.
The no-observer benchmark is the acceptance gate; this must not slow the hot path.
Progress is not a partial result: the all-or-nothing contract stays.

title: test: mutation score gate with a committed baseline
description: Run the mutation suite in CI against a committed score per package and fail when the score drops.
why: The `mutation/` module exists and mutation testing is the stronger signal than coverage, as the coverage floors themselves say. Run by hand it tells nobody anything over time: a test deleted today lowers the score and no one finds out.
criteria: A baseline score per package is committed with the measurement that produced it.
CI fails when a score drops, and the job names the surviving mutants.
Raising a baseline requires the same commit as the tests that earned it.
The run is bounded in time, with its scope documented if it cannot cover everything.
guidance: Mutation runs are slow — scope to the signing path first and schedule the rest, saying so explicitly.
Follow `scripts/checkcov`'s shape: a committed baseline file and a checker, so this stays consistent with the coverage gate.
Never lower a baseline to go green; that is the same rule the coverage floors already carry.

title: test: fuzz across the C ABI boundary
description: A fuzz target that drives the exported C functions with arbitrary bytes and asserts no crash, no hang and no memory error.
why: Every binding reaches the library through these 11 exported functions, and all of the fuzzing to date runs against Go APIs directly. The boundary itself — pointer handling, length arguments, string ownership — is the part no fuzzer currently touches, and it is the part where a mistake is a segfault in someone else's process.
criteria: Arbitrary input to each exported function produces an error, never a crash or a hang.
The target runs under a sanitizer so a memory error fails rather than passing silently.
Findings are minimised and added to a permanent regression corpus.
The target runs in CI for a bounded time and on the nightly schedule for longer.
guidance: A Go fuzzer alone will not catch the C-side memory errors; a sanitizer build is what makes this worth doing.
Cover length and pointer arguments deliberately, including zero and mismatched lengths.
`fuzz.yml` already files issues from scheduled runs — reuse it.

title: test: fuzz the verification service's request handlers
description: Fuzz each HTTP handler with arbitrary bodies, headers and paths, asserting it always answers and never panics.
why: `server/` is the component explicitly built for untrusted input, and it is the one with no fuzzing. `hardening_test.go` covers the cases someone thought of; a handler panic in a shared service is an availability bug for every caller.
criteria: Every route is fuzzed, including malformed bodies, wrong content types and oversized headers.
A panic in any handler fails the target.
The service always returns a response, and a fuzz-found hang fails the run.
Findings become permanent regression cases.
guidance: `httptest` keeps this in-process and fast; no network is needed.
Assert on the invariant 'always answers, never panics' rather than on specific status codes.
Include the authenticated routes with a valid credential so the fuzzer gets past the door.

title: test: fuzz WebAuthn assertion and attestation parsing
description: Fuzz the assertion and attestation parsers, including the CBOR decoder, over arbitrary input.
why: These parsers consume data that arrives straight from a browser or an authenticator, which is the most hostile input the library accepts. Hand-written CBOR parsing is a classic source of out-of-range and allocation bugs, and `attestation_cbor.go` is not fuzzed at all.
criteria: Arbitrary bytes produce an error, never a panic, for every parser.
A deeply nested or huge CBOR structure is refused rather than exhausting memory.
Findings are minimised into a committed corpus.
The decode bounds applied are the documented ones, not ad hoc limits.
guidance: Nesting and length-prefix abuse are the two shapes to seed deliberately.
Reuse `internal/decodepolicy` for the bounds so all untrusted decoding shares one policy.
Seed the corpus from real assertions in the existing tests so the fuzzer starts from valid structures.

title: test: a fuzz target for every public decode entry point, enforced
description: Enumerate every exported function that decodes untrusted input and fail the build when one has no fuzz target.
why: Fuzzing has been added one target at a time, so coverage of the untrusted surface is now a matter of who remembered. A new decoder added without a target is invisible, and `internal/doccheck` already shows this repository prefers an enforcing test over a convention.
criteria: The enumeration is derived from the code, not a hand-maintained list.
A new decoding entry point with no fuzz target fails the build.
An exemption is possible but must carry a stated reason in the source.
The existing targets satisfy the check without modification.
guidance: `internal/doccheck` is the model for an enforcing meta-test; follow its structure.
Define 'decodes untrusted input' precisely in the test's doc comment, since that definition is the whole check.
Exemptions need reasons in code, as the coverage floors and the cilocal manifest both do.

title: test: property test that the canonical form is idempotent
description: Property tests asserting that canonicalising twice changes nothing, and that semantically equal entries canonicalise identically regardless of construction order.
why: `canonical.go` underpins `Equal`, the JSON representation and any fingerprint built on it. If canonicalisation is not idempotent or depends on how an entry was assembled, every one of those silently compares the wrong things, and only a property test over generated entries will find it.
criteria: Canonicalising an already-canonical entry is a no-op, over generated entries.
Two entries built in different orders that are semantically equal canonicalise to identical bytes.
Delegate trees of varying shape and depth are generated, not just flat ones.
A counterexample is minimised and committed as a regression case.
guidance: Reuse the existing delegate-tree generators from the property tests rather than writing new ones.
Order independence is the property most likely to be violated; weight generation toward reordering.
If a counterexample appears, fix the code — do not weaken the property.

title: test: property test that the planner only emits valid delegate trees
description: Generate planner inputs and assert every tree it produces passes `ValidateDelegateOrder` and the duplicate rules.
why: `planner.go` constructs delegate trees and `ValidateDelegateOrder` is what the signing path enforces. Nothing currently proves the planner cannot produce a tree the signer will then reject, which would be an internally inconsistent library failing at the last step.
criteria: Every generated plan yields a tree that validates.
Generation includes duplicate addresses across levels, which the CAP permits, and within a level, which it does not.
An input the planner cannot satisfy produces an error rather than an invalid tree.
Counterexamples are committed as regression cases.
guidance: The same address at different levels is legal; within one level it is not. Generate both deliberately.
Sort by the XDR bytes of the address, as the CAP requires and the library already does.
A planner that errors is acceptable; one that emits an invalid tree is the bug.

title: test: property test that the risk analyzer is deterministic
description: Assert the analyzer returns identical findings for the same entry across runs and regardless of the order in which equivalent structures were built.
why: The analyzer's findings reach the CLI, the browser extension and any service exposing it. A finding that appears only sometimes, or depends on map iteration order, would be worse than no analyzer: a clean result would be unreliable in a way nobody could reproduce.
criteria: Repeated analysis of one entry yields identical findings in identical order.
Equivalent entries built differently yield the same findings.
Findings are stably ordered, with the ordering documented.
Map iteration is shown not to affect output.
guidance: Go randomises map iteration, which is the most likely source of instability — run the property many times.
Sort findings explicitly rather than relying on traversal order.
Keep the finding identifiers stable; consumers match on them.

title: test: continuous benchmarking with a published history
description: Record benchmark results per commit on main, publish the series, and flag a regression against the trend rather than a single threshold.
why: `scripts/checkbench` gates against a threshold, which catches a cliff but not a steady drift. The signing path has lost a few per cent at a time before, and without a history nobody can tell when it started or which change did it.
criteria: Results are recorded per commit on main and published where they can be read over time.
A regression against the recent trend is flagged, distinctly from the existing threshold gate.
Runner variance is accounted for, with the method stated.
The series survives a rerun of the same commit without appearing to change.
guidance: Noise is the whole difficulty: say how it is handled rather than treating every bump as a regression.
Reuse `checkbench`'s parsing rather than writing a second benchmark reader.
Keep the threshold gate; this is an addition for drift, not a replacement.

title: test: allocation budget for every public API call
description: Assert a committed allocation count per public operation and fail when one grows.
why: Allocations have already been reduced once in the deep-copy path, and nothing stops them coming back. The deep-copy-on-every-call rule makes this library allocation-heavy by design, so allocation count is the metric that matters for a server signing thousands of entries.
criteria: A committed budget per operation, with the measurement that set it.
CI fails when an operation exceeds its budget.
Lowering a budget is a normal change; raising one needs a stated reason in the commit.
The budgets cover each credential arm separately.
guidance: `testing.AllocsPerRun` or the benchmark's alloc counters give stable numbers; pick one and be consistent.
Per-arm budgets matter: the delegates arm legitimately allocates more.
Follow the coverage floors' convention of a reason recorded beside each number.

title: test: fault injection for remote and KMS signers
description: A harness that injects timeouts, partial responses, connection resets and malformed payloads into every network-backed signer and asserts correct behaviour.
why: Every remote signer is tested against a well-behaved fake, so they are proved to work when nothing goes wrong. The failures that matter in production — a truncated response, a reset mid-read — are exactly what no test produces, and the no-partial-result rule is most likely to break there.
criteria: Each network-backed signer is driven through timeout, reset, partial response and malformed payload.
No injected failure produces a partial result or a non-terminal error misreported as terminal.
Retry and breaker behaviour is asserted, not just the final error.
The harness is reusable so a new signer inherits the cases.
guidance: Make it a conformance dimension in `signertest` so new signers get it automatically.
A truncated-but-parseable response is the nastiest case; include it explicitly.
Assert the no-partial-result invariant on every path, since that is the library's standing rule.

title: test: run the whole suite under the race detector in CI
description: A CI job that runs the full test suite with `-race`, with its runtime bounded and its scope stated.
why: There is concurrency in batch signing, the signer cache, the nonce tracker and the coordinator, and `-race` is run ad hoc at best. A data race in the nonce tracker is a correctness bug in a replay guard, which is not something to discover from production behaviour.
criteria: The full suite runs with `-race` in CI and failures block the merge.
The job's runtime is bounded, and any excluded package is named with a reason.
At least one existing concurrent path is confirmed covered by the job.
A deliberately racy test is shown to fail the job, then removed.
guidance: `-race` is several times slower; schedule it or parallelise rather than making every pull request wait.
Show the deliberate race failing in the pull request, as the golden-vector gate does, then revert it.
Name exclusions explicitly; a silently skipped package makes the job misleading.

title: test: detect and quarantine flaky tests
description: Re-run failures to identify flakes, record them in a tracked list, and report the flake rate rather than letting a rerun hide it.
