why: This repository has already been bitten by intermittent failures — the macOS binding crash in #518 passes about one run in five. An unmanaged flake trains everyone to rerun CI, which is how a real intermittent bug gets ignored for months.
criteria: A failure that passes on rerun is recorded as a flake rather than silently passing.
Flake rates are reported per test over time.
A test exceeding a threshold is quarantined with a tracking issue, not deleted.
Quarantine is visible in the run summary so it cannot be forgotten.
guidance: Never auto-retry without recording: a silent retry is how flakes become permanent.
A quarantined test still runs and still reports; it just does not block.
#518 is the obvious first entry and a good test of the mechanism.

title: test: coverage floors for error paths specifically
description: Measure coverage of error-returning branches separately from overall statement coverage, with its own floors.
why: The per-package floors are satisfied largely by happy paths, which is normal and also the opposite of what matters here: this library's value is in refusing correctly. A package can sit at 85% with most of its error branches never executed.
criteria: Error-path coverage is measured and reported separately from statement coverage.
Floors are set per package from a measurement, with reasons recorded.
The signing path carries a strictly higher error-path floor than the rest.
The checker explains which error branches are uncovered, not just a number.
guidance: Extend `scripts/checkcov` rather than adding a second tool; it already owns the floors file.
Define the metric precisely in the doc comment — 'error path' needs to mean one thing.
Naming the uncovered branches is what makes this actionable rather than another number to satisfy.

title: test: minimise the fuzz corpus and keep a permanent regression set
description: Minimise each fuzz corpus, keep every historical finding as a permanent regression case, and separate the two in CI.
why: Corpora grow until the fuzz job spends its budget re-executing near-duplicates, which quietly reduces fuzzing to a slow unit-test run. Separately, a minimised input that once found a real bug must never be dropped, and nothing distinguishes those today.
criteria: Each corpus is minimised and the reduction is reported.
Every historical finding is kept in a regression set that always runs, separate from the exploration corpus.
Minimisation cannot drop a regression case, asserted by a test.
The fuzz job runs the regression set first, before exploring.
guidance: `cmd/gencorpus` already builds corpora; extend it rather than adding another tool.
The regression set is sacred: it is the only record that a class of bug existed.
Report the before and after sizes so the benefit is visible.

title: test: snapshot tests for the tree renderer and the TUI
description: Golden-file snapshots of the renderer's and TUI's output for a set of entries, including wide and deep trees.
why: `treerender.go` and `tui.go` are how a human decides whether to sign, so their output is a security surface: a truncated or misaligned delegate tree can hide a node. They are currently checked, if at all, by reading them, which is the one method that does not survive a refactor.
criteria: Snapshots cover a flat tree, a deep tree, a wide tree and one with duplicate addresses across levels.
A rendering change fails the test and shows a readable diff.
Snapshots are regenerated by a documented command, never edited by hand.
Output is asserted to contain every address in the entry, so nothing can be silently omitted.
guidance: The 'every address appears' assertion is the one with security value — write it as a property, not just a snapshot.
Keep snapshots small enough to review in a diff.
Follow the golden-vector rule: a snapshot is regenerated, never hand-edited.

title: test: generate golden vectors across several JS SDK versions
description: Generate the vector set under more than one pinned `@stellar/stellar-sdk` version and assert the bytes agree.
why: The vectors are the correctness gate and they come from exactly one pinned version, so a change in the reference implementation is indistinguishable from a change in ours. Agreement across two versions is what tells us the bytes are protocol-defined rather than an artefact of one release.
criteria: Vectors are generated under at least two pinned versions and compared byte for byte.
A disagreement fails loudly and is reported rather than resolved by picking one.
Each version is pinned exactly, with its lockfile committed.
The generator still refuses to run on an unpinned version.
guidance: A disagreement is a finding to report, not a vector to edit — the standing rule is that vectors are never hand-edited.
Keep the current pin as the primary and add the second as a cross-check, so the gate does not get weaker.
The CI drift check must cover both generations.

title: test: rehearse a protocol upgrade against the next host version
description: Run the e2e scenarios against a local host built for the next protocol version, so an upgrade's effect on existing entries is known before the network votes.
why: Protocol 28 arrived during this project and the library's compatibility was established after the fact. The next upgrade will be the same unless entries are tested against the new host beforehand, and the local quickstart makes that possible without waiting for a public network.
criteria: The scenarios run against a host image for the next protocol version.
A behaviour change is reported per scenario, with the raw host error.
The job is scheduled or manual and does not block pull requests.
Results are recorded with the host version and date.
guidance: The local quickstart harness already exists; reuse it rather than standing up another environment.
Report rather than adapt: a behaviour change needs a human decision, not an automatic fix.
Record the image digest, since 'next version' moves.

title: feat(protocol): generate preimages from the Rust host as a third reference
description: Produce the preimage and payload for each vector using `rs-soroban-env` directly, and compare against the Go library and the JS SDK.
why: The JS SDK is the reference today, but it is an independent reimplementation of the same specification, so a shared misreading between it and this library is invisible. `rs-soroban-env` is what the network actually runs, which makes it the authority rather than a peer.
criteria: Each vector's preimage and payload are produced from the Rust host and compared with both other implementations.
A three-way disagreement fails and reports which implementation differs.
The Rust dependency is pinned exactly with its lockfile committed.
The comparison runs in CI, or is scheduled with its skip reason reported.
guidance: Read the host's preimage construction and cite the file and function; do not reimplement from the CAP text.
Report disagreements; never change a vector to make three implementations agree.
A Rust toolchain is already pinned for the contracts — reuse that pin.

title: feat(protocol): report the nonce ledger entry a signature will consume
description: Compute the ledger key for the nonce entry an address credential will consume, so it can be included in a footprint and checked for existence.
why: The host consumes a nonce entry when it verifies an address credential, and that entry must be in the transaction's footprint. A caller assembling a transaction by hand has no way to derive the key, so they either over-provision the footprint or discover the omission as an on-chain failure after fees.
criteria: The ledger key is derived for both CAP-71 arms and the legacy arm.
The derivation is checked against a real entry observed on testnet.
A nonce already consumed is distinguishable from one that is free.
The key's construction cites the host source it was read from.
guidance: Read the key construction from `rs-soroban-env` and cite it; deriving it from the CAP text is how this gets subtly wrong.
Verify against a live testnet transaction rather than only unit tests — this is an on-chain fact.
Keep it offline and pure; fetching whether a nonce exists belongs in `rpcflow`.

title: feat(protocol): compatibility checker for entries across protocol versions
description: Given an entry and a target protocol version, report whether it would be accepted, rejected, or accepted with different semantics.
why: The third category is the dangerous one and nothing addresses it: an entry that is structurally valid on two versions but means something different on each. Protocol 28 added address binding, which is exactly that kind of change, and a caller submitting to a mixed-version environment has no tool to ask the question.
criteria: Three outcomes are distinguished: accepted, rejected and accepted-with-different-semantics.
The semantics category is justified per case against a cited protocol source.
Nested delegates are considered, not just the top-level arm.
A test covers each arm against each supported version.
guidance: Cite CAP-71-01 and CAP-71-02 for each semantic difference; an uncited claim here is a guess.
Reuse `protocolmatrix.go`'s data rather than duplicating it.
Fail closed: an unknown combination is 'unknown', never 'accepted'.

title: feat(protocol): check an entry corresponds to the operation it accompanies
description: Verify that an entry's root invocation matches the `InvokeHostFunction` operation it is attached to, and report any divergence.
why: An envelope carries operations and entries side by side, and nothing checks they agree. An entry authorizing a different contract call than the operation performs is the clearest possible sign of tampering, and it is currently undetectable without reading both by hand.
criteria: The operation's host function and the entry's root invocation are compared field by field.
A mismatch is reported with the field path, not as one opaque difference.
An entry with no corresponding operation, and an operation with no entry, are both reported.
Tests cover a matching envelope and a tampered one for each arm.
guidance: `envelope.go` already extracts entries from an envelope; extend it rather than re-parsing.
`diff.go`'s path-reporting style is the right output shape here.
Source-account entries are still subject to this check and must not be exempted.

title: feat(protocol): exhaustive vectors over arm and function-type combinations
description: A generated vector for every combination of the four credential arms and the three authorized function types, with a test that fails when a combination is missing.
why: There are four arms and three function types — `ContractFn`, `CreateContractHostFn` and `CreateContractV2HostFn` — and the vector set covers the combinations that came up rather than the matrix. The uncovered cells are where a reporting or preimage bug would sit undetected.
criteria: Every legal combination has a vector, and illegal combinations are documented as such.
A test enumerates the matrix and fails on a missing cell.
The vectors are generated by the pinned JS SDK, not hand-written.
The CI drift check covers the new vectors.
guidance: The three function types are what the SDK's xdr package defines; enumerate from the source rather than from memory.
The enumerating test is the point: it keeps the matrix complete as arms are added.
If a combination cannot be constructed, record why in the test rather than omitting it silently.

title: feat(protocol): map host rejection reasons to library errors
description: A documented, tested mapping from the host's authorization failure messages to the library's typed errors, so an on-chain rejection can be explained.
why: When a submission fails, the operator gets a host error string and has to guess which local condition caused it. The library knows about expiration, nonce reuse, ordering and signature shape, but there is no bridge between the two vocabularies, which makes a failed submission far harder to diagnose than it needs to be.
criteria: Each mapped host reason cites the host source where the message is produced.
An unmapped host error is reported as unmapped rather than guessed at.
At least the expiration, nonce, ordering and signature-shape failures are covered.
An e2e scenario produces each mapped failure and the mapping is asserted against the real error.
guidance: Drive the mapping from real failures in e2e, not from reading the host and hoping.
Host messages change between versions — record the version each mapping was observed under.
Never guess: an unmapped error must say so, since a confident wrong explanation is worse than none.

title: feat(protocol): establish and enforce the host's delegate tree limits
description: Determine the host's actual limits on delegate tree depth and breadth, document them with their source, and refuse an entry that exceeds them before it is signed.
why: `WithDelegates` accepts arbitrarily deep and wide trees. If the host has a limit, a signature over an over-limit tree is wasted work that fails on chain after fees; if it does not, the resource cost still grows and the library should say so. Either way the current silence is the problem.
criteria: The limits, or their absence, are established from the host source and cited.
An entry exceeding a limit is refused with a typed error before signing.
The documented limits and the enforced ones cannot diverge, asserted by a test.
An e2e scenario confirms the behaviour at the boundary on testnet.
guidance: Read the host rather than inferring from behaviour, then confirm with e2e at the boundary.
If there is no hard limit, document the resource cost instead and do not invent one.
Coordinate with the decode bounds so there is one policy, not two.

title: feat(protocol): validate every canonical ordering rule an entry must satisfy
description: Enumerate every ordering and canonicality rule the host enforces on an entry, and validate all of them in one place.
why: Delegate ordering is validated and multisig key ordering is enforced in the signer, but these were each added when someone noticed them. There is no enumeration of what the host requires, so nobody can say whether the list is complete — and a missed rule means an entry that fails on chain after fees.
criteria: The rules are enumerated with a citation to the host source for each.
All of them are validated through one entry point before signing.
A rule the library cannot check offline is documented as such rather than omitted.
Tests cover a violation of each rule.
guidance: The enumeration with citations is the deliverable; the validation is mostly already written.
Reuse `ValidateDelegateOrder` and the multisig ordering check rather than reimplementing them.
Be explicit about what cannot be checked offline; an incomplete list presented as complete is the risk.

title: feat(protocol): muxed account handling audited across the whole surface
description: Audit every place an address is parsed, formatted or reported for muxed handling, and make the behaviour consistent and tested.
why: `ParseAddress` refuses `M…` for credentials, which is correct, but muxed addresses can legitimately appear inside invocation arguments. The reporting, diff and risk paths each handle them by whatever their own code does, so a muxed address may be reported inconsistently or dropped, and a dropped recipient in a report is a security problem.
criteria: Every address-handling site is enumerated and its muxed behaviour stated.
A muxed address in an invocation argument is reported in full, never truncated to its underlying account.
Credentials still refuse muxed addresses, unchanged.
Tests cover a muxed address in an argument through inspect, diff and the renderer.
guidance: Grep for every address formatting site before changing any of them; the audit is the work.
Never silently convert a muxed address to its underlying account in a report — that hides the recipient.
Keep the credentials rule exactly as it is; this is about arguments.

title: feat(protocol): verify the invocation tree the host would reconstruct
description: Compare the library's view of an invocation tree against the tree the host reports during simulation, and fail on divergence.
why: #309 reconstructs the `__check_auth` context the host would pass. The adjacent question is whether the library's reading of the whole tree matches the host's, including sub-invocation order and depth. If it does not, every report and every risk finding is describing a different tree from the one being authorized.
criteria: The library's tree and the host's reported tree are compared structurally.
A divergence fails with the path at which the trees differ.
The comparison covers nested sub-invocations at more than two levels.
The check runs against recorded simulation responses offline and against testnet in e2e.
guidance: `rpcflow/rpcfixture` makes the offline half hermetic; use it for the regression test.
Compare structure and order, not formatting.
If the trees diverge, report it rather than adapting the library's reading to match — the cause matters.

title: feat(api): risk rules loaded from configuration
description: Let the analyzer's rules be supplied as configuration, so an operator can add a rule without changing the library.
why: `risk.go`'s findings are compiled in, and `policy/rules.go` already shows this repository expresses rules as data. Every operator has at least one organisation-specific rule — an address allowlist, an amount ceiling — and today the only ways to get one are to fork or to re-implement the analyzer.
criteria: Rules can be supplied as configuration and are evaluated alongside the built-in ones.
A malformed rule set is refused at load time with the offending rule named, never silently skipped.
Configured rules cannot suppress a built-in finding.
Tests cover a valid rule set, a malformed one and an attempt to suppress a built-in finding.
guidance: Reuse `policy/rules.go`'s vocabulary rather than inventing a second rule language in the same repository.
Fail closed at load time: a rule that silently does not apply is worse than no rule.
Built-in findings are a floor, not a default to be overridden — enforce that in code.

title: chore: custom linters for the repository's own invariants
description: Analyzers that enforce the rules this repository states in prose: no mutation of caller input, no logging in library code, no `panic` outside tests, no `math/rand`, no floats.
why: These rules are in CLAUDE.md and the coding standards, and they are currently enforced by review. Review has already missed each of them at least once; the no-mutation rule in particular is invisible in a diff because it looks like ordinary field assignment on a struct the caller still owns.
criteria: An analyzer exists per rule and runs in CI.
Each analyzer is tested with a violating and a compliant fixture.
A violation fails the build with the file, line and the rule's rationale.
Exemptions require a directive with a stated reason in the source.
guidance: `golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis` is the framework and needs no new direct dependency beyond the tools module.
`internal/doccheck` is the precedent for enforcing a repository convention with a test.
Start with no-logging and no-panic, which are mechanical; the no-mutation rule is the hard one and may need the deep-copy call as its signal.

title: chore: branch protection and rulesets as code with drift detection
description: Keep the required checks, review requirements and bypass actors in a committed file, and fail a scheduled job when the live configuration differs.
why: The required checks and the bypass list are security configuration that currently lives only in the GitHub UI, where a change leaves no trace in the repository. A merge-queue app holding a permanent bypass, or a required check quietly removed, would be invisible in review — and this repository has already had both questions come up.
criteria: The intended configuration is committed and human-readable.
A scheduled job compares live against committed and reports any difference.
Bypass actors are part of the comparison, not just the check list.
A deliberate drift is shown to be detected, then reverted.
guidance: Report rather than auto-apply: a job that rewrites protection rules is itself a risk.
Include both repositories in the organisation so the comparison is complete.
Show the detection working in the pull request, as the golden-vector gate does.

title: ci: secret scanning across the full history
description: Scan every pull request and the whole history for committed credentials, with an allowlist for the repository's deterministic test keys.
why: The repository derives test keys from public labels deliberately, so a naive scanner reports them on every run and gets ignored, which is worse than not running it. A real key committed once stays in the history even after a revert, so a history scan is the only way to know the repository is clean.
criteria: Pull requests and the full history are both scanned.
The deterministic test keys are allowlisted by their derivation, not by pattern.
A finding fails the run and names the commit and file.
The allowlist is documented so nobody widens it casually.
guidance: The allowlist design is the whole difficulty: too broad and it hides a real key.
The test keys come from `sha256(label)` — allowlist by that construction rather than by matching key-shaped strings.
A history scan runs once on a schedule, not per pull request.

title: ci: advisory scanning across every ecosystem the repository ships
description: Scan Go, npm, Rust, Python and Maven dependencies against advisory databases on every pull request and on a schedule.
why: Dependency review covers the Go module's graph. The repository now ships five language bindings, each with its own lockfile and its own dependency tree, and none of those are scanned. A vulnerable transitive dependency in the Node or Python binding reaches users through a published package.
criteria: Every committed lockfile is scanned, and a new lockfile with no scan coverage fails the build.
Findings are reported with severity and the path to the dependency.
The scheduled run covers published artifacts, not only the source tree.
A scanner failure is reported rather than treated as a pass.
guidance: The enforcing check — a lockfile with no scanner — is what keeps this complete as bindings are added.
`osv-scanner` handles most of these ecosystems in one pass.
Never let a scanner error exit zero; that is how scanning quietly stops.

title: chore: license inventory across every ecosystem
description: Produce a license inventory for all five bindings and the Go module, fail on a license outside an allowed set, and publish the inventory with each release.
why: The project is Apache-2.0 and consumers with a compliance process need to know what they are pulling in transitively. With five ecosystems there is no single command that answers this, and a copyleft transitive dependency in one binding would be found by a consumer's audit rather than ours.
criteria: An inventory is generated per ecosystem and combined into one document.
A license outside the allowed set fails the build and names the dependency.
The allowed set is committed with its rationale.
The inventory is published with each release.
guidance: Decide the allowed set deliberately and write down why; an arbitrary list causes arguments later.
An unknown or missing license must fail rather than pass, since unknown is the common case for small packages.
This pairs with the SBOM work; share the generation where possible.

title: ci: bring the pipeline's runtime within a stated budget
description: Measure the pull-request pipeline's critical path, restructure the job graph to fit a stated budget, and fail when a change pushes it over.
why: There are two dozen workflows now, and the cost report shows where the minutes go but nothing bounds them. A slow pipeline gets worked around rather than waited for, which is how a red check gets merged past — the failure mode this repository has already had.
criteria: The critical path is measured and published.
A stated budget is enforced and a change exceeding it fails with an explanation.
Advisory and path-filtered workflows are excluded from the budget and that exclusion is explicit.
No check is removed or weakened to meet the budget.
guidance: `cost-report.yml` already gathers per-workflow duration; build on it rather than measuring again.
The last criterion is the important one: this must not become an excuse to delete coverage.
Parallelism and caching are the levers; `scripts/cilocal`'s manifest already describes what each job needs.

title: feat(cmd): Windows support for the CLI, built and smoke-tested
description: Build and test the CLI on Windows, fixing the path, console and shell assumptions that break there, with a smoke test in CI.
why: `scripts/cilocal` already carries Windows-specific logic for finding bash, and Wave 11's contributor ran their verification on a Windows host, so Windows developers are already here. The CLI is not built or tested there, so whether it works at all is unknown, and the completion and exec-signer paths are the obvious suspects.
criteria: The CLI builds for Windows in CI and a smoke test runs every subcommand.
Path handling, line endings and the exec-based signer work or are documented as unsupported with a reason.
The release publishes a Windows binary, or the documentation states plainly that it does not.
Shell completions either work on PowerShell or are documented as unavailable.
guidance: Decide and state the support level first; a half-supported platform is worse than a documented unsupported one.
The exec-signer and completion tests are where this will fail; look there before assuming it works.
The bindings' dlopen-based loading is explicitly Linux and macOS only — do not imply Windows support for those.

title: ci: a pre-release channel with a canary install path
description: Publish pre-release versions from a tag suffix to every channel, so a release can be exercised by real consumers before it becomes current.
why: The release pipeline publishes to a container registry, npm and a docs site in one step, and the first consumer of a mistake is everyone. A pre-release channel lets a version be installed deliberately without becoming the default for anyone who does not ask for it.
criteria: A pre-release tag publishes to every channel without moving any 'latest' pointer.
The documented install commands for the pre-release channel are tested in CI.
A pre-release is clearly marked in every channel's metadata.
Promotion to a full release does not rebuild the artifacts.
guidance: Not moving 'latest' is the property that matters; verify it per channel rather than assuming.
Promoting without rebuilding keeps the reproducibility and provenance claims intact.
Follow the existing tag-guard pattern so a pre-release cannot be published from an untagged commit.

title: ci: aggregate every scanner's output into code scanning
description: Have every analysis job emit SARIF and upload it, so findings appear in one place with history rather than in job logs.
why: CodeQL reports into code scanning; the supply-chain scan, the custom linters and the advisory scanners each print to a job log that nobody reads unless it fails. A finding that does not block a merge is effectively invisible, which is the wrong outcome for a warning-level security finding.
criteria: Each analysis job emits SARIF and uploads it.
Findings carry a stable rule identifier so they can be tracked across runs.
A warning appears in code scanning without failing the build; a blocking finding still fails it.
The upload failing is itself reported.
guidance: `scripts/supply-chain-scan.sh` already separates blocking from warning severities — map that distinction onto SARIF levels.
Stable rule identifiers are what make history useful; assign them deliberately.
Keep the human-readable output too; the SARIF is an addition.

title: ci: a release dry run that exercises the whole pipeline
description: A manually triggered run that performs every release step against throwaway destinations, so the pipeline is proved before a real tag.
why: `release.yml` is the longest and least-exercised workflow, and it only ever runs on a real tag, which means its failures are discovered mid-release. This repository has already found a release step that had never succeeded — the tool-version step that exited 127 on every tag.
criteria: Every step runs, including the publish steps, against throwaway destinations.
The dry run cannot write to any real registry, repository or release.
A step that cannot be dry-run is named, with its reason.
The dry run is part of the release checklist.
guidance: Enforce the throwaway destinations structurally, not by convention — a dry run that publishes for real is the failure to design out.
Naming the un-dry-runnable steps is valuable on its own.
The existing release checklist is where this belongs; wire it in rather than leaving it optional.

title: chore: version the documentation site per release
description: Publish a versioned copy of the documentation per release alongside the current one, with a switcher and a canonical URL policy.
why: The site publishes from main, so someone on the released version reads documentation for unreleased behaviour. For a library whose documentation states protocol semantics and API contracts, that mismatch produces confident wrong conclusions.
criteria: Each release publishes a versioned copy that remains available.
A version switcher is present and the current version is unambiguous.
Canonical URLs point at the current release, not at main.
Older versions carry a notice that they are not current.
guidance: `scripts/docsite` already builds the site; this is about publication layout.
Decide the retention policy explicitly or the site grows forever.
Set canonical tags properly or search results will keep sending people to stale pages.

title: feat(cmd): plugin mechanism for out-of-tree subcommands
description: Discover and dispatch to external `soroauth-*` executables on PATH, so an organisation can add a subcommand without forking.
why: The CLI has accumulated many subcommands and the non-goals are explicit about what it will not absorb — key management, wallets, bespoke policy. A plugin mechanism is how those stay out of the binary while remaining usable, and it is the standard pattern for this.
criteria: An external `soroauth-foo` is discoverable and invocable as `soroauth foo`.
`--help` lists discovered plugins separately from built-in subcommands.
A plugin cannot shadow a built-in subcommand.
No secret is passed to a plugin except through the documented environment-variable mechanism.
guidance: Built-ins must win: shadowing `sign` would be a security problem, so enforce it rather than documenting it.
Keep the CLI's existing discipline — never a secret as an argument — across the plugin boundary too.
Document the contract so a plugin author knows what is stable.

title: chore: enforce artifact and cache retention policies
description: Set a deliberate retention per artifact kind, prune caches on a schedule, and report storage use.
why: Workflows upload prebuilds, parity reports, coverage data and vector artifacts with whatever retention they happened to specify. Beyond cost, a long-lived artifact containing a build of untrusted pull-request code is a liability nobody is tracking.
criteria: Every upload specifies a retention, and one without it fails a check.
Caches are pruned on a schedule and storage use is reported.
Artifacts from pull-request runs have a shorter retention than those from main.
The policy is documented with its reasoning.
guidance: The enforcing check is the durable part; a one-time cleanup regresses immediately.
Reuse `cost-report.yml`'s reporting shape for storage.
Treat pull-request artifacts as untrusted and say so in the policy.

title: chore: reconcile filed issues against the committed backlog
description: A mode that compares a committed backlog against the issues actually filed and reports missing, extra, retitled and mislabelled ones.
why: The backlog is committed as the source of truth and the issues are filed from it, after which the two drift: an issue gets retitled, a label is dropped, a points label disagrees with the backlog. With several hundred issues across waves, nobody can check that by hand, and the points total is what the programme is measured on.
criteria: The reconciliation reports missing, extra, retitled and mislabelled issues.
The points total from the labels is compared against the backlog's and any difference is reported.
The mode is read-only and changes nothing.
It runs against a previous wave and its output is included in the pull request.
guidance: Read-only by default; an auto-fix that retitles a contributor's issue would be worse than the drift.
Match on title first and fall back to the issue body's backlog identifier, since titles are what get edited.
`scripts/wave_issues.py` already validates a backlog and skips by title — reuse both.

title: docs: incident runbook for a failed or suspicious signature
description: A runbook for the operational emergencies: a submission rejected on chain, a signature nobody can account for, a signer behaving unexpectedly, a suspected key compromise.
why: There is documentation for what verification establishes and what to do when a submission fails, but nothing for the case where something has already gone wrong and someone is deciding whether to stop signing. That decision gets made under time pressure, which is the worst moment to be reading the API reference.
criteria: Each scenario has detection signals, immediate containment steps and an escalation path.
Every command in the runbook is one that exists and is tested as a documented snippet.
The limits are stated plainly: what the library's records can and cannot tell you after the fact.
It links to the audit record and transcript features rather than restating them.
guidance: Write it for someone under pressure: short steps, no background reading required.
Verify every command against the current CLI; a runbook with a stale flag is actively harmful.
Be honest about the forensic limits — without an audit log, some questions simply cannot be answered.

title: docs: key compromise playbook
description: What to do when a signing key is believed compromised, for each custody model the repository supports.
why: A Stellar account's address is its public key, so a compromised key cannot be rotated the way a password can — the response is different for a classic multisig account, a threshold account and a custom account contract. That difference is exactly what an operator will not work out correctly during an incident.
criteria: A procedure per custody model, stating what can and cannot be recovered.
The irreversibility is stated plainly where it applies.
Preventive measures are separated from incident response.
Any claim about on-chain behaviour cites the protocol source or an e2e result.
guidance: Do not imply recovery is possible where it is not; false hope here costs money.
Cover the threshold case properly — share refresh and DKG change what is possible.
Keep it separate from `SECURITY.md`, which is about reporting vulnerabilities in this library, and cross-link the two.

title: docs: a getting-started guide per language binding
description: A guide per binding — C, Node, Python, JVM, Rust, wasm — taking a reader from install to a signed entry in their own language.
why: Each binding has a README describing its build, which is written for someone working on the binding rather than using it. A Python or JVM developer currently has to read Go documentation and infer the mapping, which is the main reason the bindings see little use.
criteria: Each guide goes from install to a signed entry with complete, runnable code.
Every snippet is compiled or executed in CI, so none can go stale.
Error handling is shown in the language's own idiom, not translated from Go.
Each guide states what that binding does not support.
guidance: The repository already verifies README snippets compile — extend that mechanism rather than trusting review.
Idiomatic error handling is the part most worth getting right; a Go-shaped API in Python will not be used.
State the gaps honestly: several bindings cannot be installed from a package registry yet.

title: docs: trust boundaries across the whole system
description: A document identifying every trust boundary the project now spans — FFI, HTTP, gRPC, browser, cloud KMS, multi-party — and what each one assumes.
why: The threat model was written when this was a Go library. It now crosses six language boundaries, two network services and a browser, and each of those was added with its own local reasoning. Nobody can currently answer which assumptions hold across the whole system, which is the question an adopter's security review asks first.
criteria: Every boundary is identified with what crosses it and what is assumed about each side.
Assumptions that are not enforced in code are marked as such.
Each boundary links to the code and the tests that defend it.
The document states what is explicitly out of scope.
guidance: Marking unenforced assumptions is the most valuable part; that list is the real risk register.
Build on the existing threat model rather than replacing it.
Link to the FFI threading contract and the service hardening posture instead of restating them.

title: docs: published compatibility and support matrix per release
description: A generated matrix of Go versions, SDK versions, protocol versions, binding language versions and platforms, published with each release.
why: This information exists in `go.mod`, `docs/sdk-support.md`, the binding manifests and the protocol matrix, and the pieces have disagreed before — the Go floor moved twice without the documentation following. An adopter asking what is supported has to assemble it from five places and may get a stale answer.
criteria: The matrix is generated from the authoritative files, never hand-maintained.
A disagreement between the matrix and any source file fails the build.
It is published with each release and kept with the versioned documentation.
Support levels are distinguished: tested, best-effort and unsupported.
guidance: Generation is the point: a hand-written matrix is how this went stale before.
`internal/doccheck` already fails the build when documented versions disagree with `go.mod` — extend it.
Be explicit about best-effort versus tested; several bindings and platforms are not covered by CI.

title: docs: a worked air-gapped signing procedure
description: An end-to-end procedure for signing on a machine that has never been networked, with the commands, the file exchange and the verification steps on both sides.
why: This is the custody model with the strongest guarantees and the least guidance. Operators attempting it today improvise the transfer, and the improvisation is where a signature gets applied to a different entry than the one reviewed.
criteria: The procedure covers both machines, including what is verified before signing and after returning.
The payload-binding check is explicit, so a substituted entry is caught.
Every command is tested as a documented snippet.
What the air gap does and does not protect is stated.
guidance: The verification step on the offline machine is the security property; make it unmissable.
This pairs with the file-exchange signer work; write the document against the real commands once they exist.
Do not overclaim: an air gap does not protect against a compromised offline machine, and the document should say so.

title: docs: operating a threshold or multi-party signing setup
description: An operations guide for threshold signing: generating shares, distributing them, refreshing, handling an unavailable participant, and recovering from a lost share.
why: `frost/` and `coordinator.go` provide the mechanism, and the hard part of threshold signing is operational, not cryptographic. A team that loses a share or has a participant go offline during a round has no guidance, and the wrong improvisation there can make an account permanently unusable.
criteria: Covers generation, distribution, refresh, unavailability and share loss.
States clearly at what point an account becomes unrecoverable.
Each procedure's commands are tested.
Accuracy is tied to the implementation, with a test or check that fails if they diverge.
guidance: The unrecoverable threshold is the most important fact in the document; put it near the top.
Write it against the real API, not the intended one; note anything the implementation does not yet support.
Coordinate with the DKG and refresh work so the document does not describe unbuilt features as available.

title: docs: capacity planning for the verification service
description: Measured throughput and latency per entry shape, with the resulting sizing guidance and the limits that bound it.
why: There are benchmarks for the signing path and metrics in the service, but nothing connecting them to how much hardware a given request rate needs. A delegate tree costs far more to verify than a simple entry, so a rate figure without an entry shape is meaningless — and that is the only kind of figure available today.
criteria: Throughput and latency are measured per entry shape, including a deep delegate tree.
Sizing guidance follows from the measurements and names the hardware they were taken on.
The work limits and rate limits are related to the numbers.
Every figure carries its date and the version measured.
guidance: Reuse the existing benchmarks rather than producing a separate set that will drift.
Date and version every number, as the README's evidence rule already requires.
Report the worst case as well as the typical one; capacity planning on an average is how services fall over.

title: docs: Go doc examples for canonical.go
description: Runnable `Example` functions for the canonical-form helpers, in the style of the existing example files.
why: `canonical.go` underpins `Equal`, the JSON representation and the diff tooling, and `pkg.go.dev` shows its signatures with no worked use. Canonicalisation is also the kind of operation whose point is unclear from a signature alone.
criteria: At least one example showing two differently-built but equal entries canonicalising identically.
Output assertions use real values from a committed golden vector, not invented ones.
File-scoped constants, so the file cannot collide with another example file's identifiers.
`go test ./...` passes with the examples' output verified.
guidance: Read `inspect_example_test.go` and follow it exactly; consistency across example files is the point.
Run the test to get the real output rather than predicting it — a guessed `// Output:` is the usual failure.
Keep each example short enough to read on `pkg.go.dev` without scrolling.

title: docs: Go doc examples for Equal and Clone
description: Runnable examples for `Equal` and `Clone`, showing the deep-copy guarantee.
why: `Equal` and `Clone` landed after the Wave 9 doc-example pass, so they have none. `Clone`'s whole value is that mutating the copy cannot affect the original, which an example demonstrates far better than a sentence.
criteria: An example mutates a clone and shows the original unchanged.
An example shows `Equal` returning false for entries differing only in signature.
Values come from a committed golden vector.
`go test ./...` passes with output verified.
guidance: Follow the existing example files' structure exactly.
The mutation example is the valuable one — make the unchanged original visible in the output.
Use file-scoped constants to avoid identifier collisions.

title: docs: Go doc examples for the nonce tracker
description: Runnable examples showing a nonce being recorded and a reuse being refused.
why: A replay guard is only useful if callers wire it in, and `noncetracker.go` has no example showing where it sits in a signing flow. Its API is small enough that the gap is purely documentation.
criteria: An example records a nonce and shows a second use refused.
The example makes clear the tracker is per-process unless given durable storage.
Output assertions are verified by running the test.
`go test ./...` passes.
guidance: Follow the existing example files.
State the in-memory limitation in the example's comment; that is the thing people get wrong.
Keep it short — this is an illustration, not a tutorial.

title: docs: Go doc examples for the signer chain
description: Runnable examples for the signer chain's fallback and quorum behaviour.
why: `chain.go` has two distinct behaviours — fallback and quorum — and which one a given construction produces is not obvious from the signature. That ambiguity is exactly what gets misconfigured, and a chain that silently falls back when quorum was intended is a security problem.
criteria: One example per behaviour, fallback and quorum.
The quorum example shows what happens when quorum is not met.
Deterministic test signers are used so the output is stable.
`go test ./...` passes with output verified.
guidance: Derive test keys the repository's way, `keypair.FromRawSeed(sha256(label))`, so output is deterministic.
Make the not-met case explicit; that is the behaviour worth documenting.
Follow the existing example files' style.

title: docs: Go doc examples for the threshold signer
description: Runnable examples for the threshold signer interface, showing a successful signature and a below-threshold refusal.
why: Threshold signing is the hardest part of the library to adopt and has no worked example. The below-threshold case matters most: a caller needs to see that it fails cleanly rather than producing a partial signature.
criteria: An example produces a signature with enough participants.
An example shows a below-threshold attempt refused with no partial result.
Fixed test shares so the output is deterministic.
`go test ./...` passes with output verified.
guidance: Keep the share setup in the example minimal; the signing call is the subject.
The refusal example is the important one — show that nothing usable comes back.
Follow the existing example files.

title: docs: Go doc examples for the policy package
description: Runnable examples showing a policy allowing and refusing an entry.
why: `policy/` expresses rules as data, which is the right design and also the one that needs an example to be usable. Nothing on `pkg.go.dev` shows what a rule looks like, so the package is effectively undiscoverable.
criteria: An example constructs a policy and shows an entry allowed and one refused.
The refusal names the rule that refused it.
Values come from a committed golden vector.
`go test ./...` passes with output verified.
guidance: Pick the simplest real rule for the example rather than demonstrating the whole vocabulary.
Show the refusal reason in the output; that is what makes the package usable.
Follow the existing example files.

title: docs: document the three authorized function types in one place
description: A short reference for `ContractFn`, `CreateContractHostFn` and `CreateContractV2HostFn`: what each authorizes and how the library reports it.
why: `doc.go` documents the four credential arms in a table, which is the single most useful thing in the package documentation. The authorized function types get no equivalent treatment although they determine what an entry actually permits, and the difference between the two create arms is a security-relevant distinction.
criteria: All three types are listed with what each authorizes.
The difference between the two create arms, including constructor arguments, is stated.
The list is derived from the SDK's `xdr` package and cites the file read.
A test fails if the SDK gains a function type the document does not mention.
guidance: Enumerate from the SDK source, not from memory; cite the file.
The enforcing test is what keeps this current — `internal/doccheck` is the precedent.
Match the style of the credential-arm table already in `doc.go`.

title: docs: document the credential arm constants
description: Doc comments on each `CredentialArm` constant explaining what the arm is, which preimage it uses and whether it is address-bound.
why: `arm.go` exports four constants that are the library's central vocabulary, and the per-constant documentation does not say which preimage variant each implies. That mapping is the thing a reader most needs and currently has to reconstruct from `preimage.go`.
criteria: Each constant documents its preimage variant and whether the address is in the signed bytes.
The CAP that defines each arm is cited.
The doc comments agree with `preimage.go`, asserted by a test or by citation.
No claim is made that any arm is deprecated.
guidance: The arm-to-preimage mapping is in `preimage.go`; read it rather than restating from the table.
Cite CAP-46-11 and CAP-71-01 as appropriate.
The legacy address arm is not deprecated — the repository's standards are explicit about that wording.

title: docs: bindings index with the install status of each language
description: One page listing all six bindings with how to install each, or stating plainly that it must be built from source.
why: There are now six bindings in varying states: the wasm package is published to npm, the others are not. A reader has to open each README to find that out, and the honest answer — that most cannot yet be installed from a registry — is not stated anywhere.
criteria: Every binding is listed with its install method or 'build from source'.
Platform support is stated per binding, including that the native bindings are Linux and macOS only.
The known macOS limitation in the Node binding is linked rather than restated.
A test fails if a new directory appears under `bindings/` without an entry.
guidance: Be accurate about what is unpublished; overstating availability wastes a reader's afternoon.
Link to #518 for the Node macOS issue rather than duplicating its content.
The enforcing test keeps the page complete as bindings are added.

title: docs: record the pre-merge supply-chain audit in CONTRIBUTING
description: Document that `scripts/supply-chain-scan.sh` runs before any merge, how to run it locally, and how to read its blocking and warning severities.
why: The scan is a required status check and a standing pre-merge step, but `CONTRIBUTING.md` does not mention it. A contributor whose pull request is held by a warning has no way to find out what the scan is or how to run it themselves.
criteria: The command is documented with how to run it against a pull request and against a working tree.
The blocking and warning severities are explained, with what to do about each.
It is stated that the exit status must be captured directly, not through a pipe.
The documented command is tested as a snippet.
guidance: The pipe caveat is worth stating: reading `$?` after a pipe gives the wrong command's status, which has caused a real mistake here.
Keep it short and point at the script's own header comment for detail.
Follow the existing CONTRIBUTING structure rather than adding a new top-level section.

title: docs: glossary entries for threshold and multi-party terms
description: Glossary entries for threshold signature, FROST, share, DKG, quorum, coordinator and participant, as this repository uses them.
why: The glossary covers Soroban authorization vocabulary well. The threshold and multi-party features added a second vocabulary with none of it defined, and several of those words — quorum in particular — already mean something different in `chain.go` than in `frost/`.
criteria: Each term is defined as this repository uses it, with the file that uses it.
Where a term has two meanings in the repository, both are given and distinguished.
Entries follow the glossary's existing format.
Terms link to the relevant package documentation.
guidance: The quorum ambiguity between `chain.go` and `frost/` is the most useful entry; do not paper over it.
Define as used, not as the literature defines it, and note any difference.
Match the existing entries' length and tone.

title: docs: document the ci-local manifest's classification vocabulary
description: Explain the manifest's terms — `requires`, `skip`, `os`, `steps`, `command`, `covered`, `bookkeeping` — and the rule that a skip is only for what a laptop cannot do.
why: The vocabulary is defined in the manifest's own `note` field, which is where a contributor finds it only after a test has already failed. Adding a workflow now fails the build until the job is classified, so the first encounter is a failure with no documentation to hand.
criteria: Each classification term is explained with when to use it.
The rule that a skip is not for making a failing check pass is stated.
The failure message a contributor sees is shown alongside what to do about it.
The `note` field and the documentation cannot disagree, asserted by a test.
guidance: Reuse the wording from the manifest's `note` rather than paraphrasing it into a second version.
Show the actual test failure text; that is what a contributor searches for.
The consistency test keeps the two copies honest.

title: chore: ignore the Node binding's prebuilds directory
description: Add `bindings/node/prebuilds/` to `.gitignore`.
why: `git check-ignore` confirms the directory is not ignored, so it shows as untracked after any local Node binding build. It appears in `git status` for every contributor who builds that binding, which is how an unrelated file ends up in a commit — something that has already happened in this repository.
criteria: `bindings/node/prebuilds/` is ignored.
`git status` is clean after a local Node binding build.
No currently tracked file becomes ignored, verified with `git check-ignore` against the tracked set.
The entry sits with the other generated-output entries and carries a comment.
guidance: Check with `git check-ignore -v` before and after; the verification is the work.
Make sure nothing in that directory is currently tracked, or ignoring it will hide real changes.
The existing generated-output section of `.gitignore` is where this belongs.

title: chore: pin the two remaining mutable action references
description: Pin `codecov/codecov-action` and the remaining `actions/upload-artifact` reference to commit SHAs, as every other action already is.
why: A tag is mutable: whoever controls it can change what runs in CI, which has write access to this repository's caches and artifacts. The repository already pins actions by SHA as a policy, and a grep shows exactly two references still on a tag, so this is a small gap in an otherwise complete control.
criteria: Both references are pinned to a full 40-character commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment.
A grep for mutable references returns nothing.
The pinned SHA is verified to be the commit the tag pointed at.
A check fails the build if a mutable reference is introduced.
guidance: Resolve the SHA from the tag and record the version in a comment, matching the existing style.
The enforcing check is what stops this recurring; one grep in a workflow is enough.
Confirm the SHA belongs to the action's repository, not a fork.

title: chore: a timeout on every CI job
description: Give every job a `timeout-minutes` and fail the build when a job is added without one.
why: Most job blocks across the workflows set no timeout, so they inherit the six-hour default. A hung job therefore burns runner minutes for hours and blocks the queue — and this project has already hit a genuinely hung test process, which is exactly the shape that triggers it.
criteria: Every job sets a timeout appropriate to its work.
A job added without one fails a check.
The e2e and devcontainer jobs keep timeouts long enough for their real runtimes.
No job's timeout is below its observed duration on main.
guidance: Take the durations from recent runs rather than guessing; too tight is worse than the default.
`ci-devcontainer.yml` already uses sixty minutes — leave long-running jobs long.
The enforcing check belongs with the other workflow meta-checks.

title: chore: a make target for the supply-chain scan
description: A `make audit` target that runs the supply-chain scan, listed in `make help`.
why: The scan is a required check and a pre-merge step, but running it means remembering the script's path and its flags. Every other routine check in this repository has a make target, and the one security check does not.
criteria: The target runs the scan and propagates its exit status unchanged.
It appears in `make help` and in `.PHONY`.
The status is not lost through a pipe.
The target is documented in CONTRIBUTING alongside the other checks.
guidance: Do not pipe the script's output in the target, or the make target reports the wrong status.
Follow the Makefile's existing comment style for a new target.
`make check-index` already lists checks — make sure this appears there too if that target enumerates them.

title: chore: a make target for the mutation suite
description: A `make mutation` target that runs the mutation module, with a documented time bound.
why: `mutation/` is a separate module with no entry point in the Makefile, so running it requires reading the module to work out how. A tool that is awkward to run does not get run, and mutation testing is the repository's own stated strongest correctness signal.
criteria: The target runs the suite and propagates its exit status.
It appears in `make help` and `.PHONY`.
The expected runtime is documented in the target's comment.
A variable allows scoping the run to one package.
guidance: Document the runtime honestly; an unexpectedly hour-long target gets cancelled and never retried.
Follow the `FUZZTIME` and `SOAKTIME` pattern for the scoping variable.
The module is separate, so the target needs the right working directory.

title: chore: issue template for a platform-specific binding failure
description: A template collecting the platform, architecture, language runtime version, binding and build method for a binding problem.
why: There are six bindings across two operating systems and two architectures, and a binding report without that context cannot be acted on. The existing templates are written for library bugs and do not ask for any of it — the macOS Node crash took a long diagnostic session partly because the relevant variables were not known up front.
criteria: The template collects operating system, architecture, runtime version, binding and whether a prebuild or source build was used.
It asks whether the problem is intermittent, and at what rate.
It links to the known-issues section so a known problem is not refiled.
It follows the existing templates' structure.
guidance: The intermittency question matters: #518 fails about one run in five and that rate was the key fact.
Keep it short — a long form does not get filled in.
Match the existing templates' YAML style.

title: chore: CODEOWNERS entries for the bindings and adapters
description: Add ownership entries for each binding and adapter directory so changes there request a review from whoever maintains them.
why: `CODEOWNERS` exists but predates the bindings and adapters, so a change to the JVM binding or a KMS adapter routes to whoever owns the root. Those are the areas where a reviewer most needs specific knowledge, and a wrongly routed review tends to be a shallow one.
criteria: Each binding and adapter directory has an entry.
The entries do not accidentally broaden ownership of the root package.
The file's syntax is validated, since a malformed entry silently matches nothing.
The pattern order is checked, as later patterns win.
guidance: Pattern order is the usual mistake: a broad root pattern placed last overrides everything above it.
A malformed CODEOWNERS fails quietly — verify through the repository's settings view or an API check.
Use teams rather than individuals where a team exists.

title: test: assert every golden vector declares the current schema version
description: A test that fails when a committed vector's `schema_version` is missing or not the current one.
why: All eighteen vectors are at version 1 today, and the schema is versioned precisely so a change is detectable. Nothing enforces it, so a regenerated or hand-added vector at a different version — or with the field absent — would be read with the wrong expectations and the mismatch would surface as a confusing byte difference.
criteria: Every vector is checked and a missing or wrong version fails with the file named.
The current version is defined in one place, not repeated per test.
The test covers any new vector automatically, with no list to maintain.
A deliberately altered vector is shown to fail the test, then reverted.
guidance: Read the directory rather than hard-coding filenames, so new vectors are covered.
Show the test failing in the pull request, as the golden-vector gate does, then revert.
Never edit a vector to satisfy a test — the standing rule is that vectors are regenerated, not hand-edited.

title: test: assert the CLI's documented exit codes match the implementation
description: A test comparing the documented exit codes against the ones the CLI actually returns.
why: The CLI has meaningful exit codes and they are documented, which makes them an interface people script against. A code changed in the implementation without the documentation following would silently break a caller's error handling, and nothing currently ties the two together.
criteria: Every documented code is produced by a real invocation in the test.
A code the CLI returns but does not document fails the test.
The documentation is parsed rather than duplicated in the test.
The diff subcommand's distinct stale-signature code is covered.
guidance: Parse the documentation so there is one source of truth, rather than restating the codes in the test.
Drive the CLI as a subprocess, so the real exit status is what is observed.
Cover both directions: documented-but-unreachable and returned-but-undocumented.

title: test: assert each binding README states its supported platforms
description: A test requiring every binding's README to state its supported operating systems, architectures and runtime versions.
why: The native bindings load a shared library with `dlopen` and are Linux and macOS only, which some READMEs say and others do not. A reader on Windows should not have to discover that by building, and a new binding should not be able to ship without stating it.
criteria: Every directory under `bindings/` must have a README with a platform-support statement.
A new binding with no statement fails the build.
The check looks for a structured section rather than matching loose prose.
The existing READMEs pass, or are updated in the same change.
guidance: `internal/doccheck` is the right home and already contains tests of this shape.
Require a recognisable heading so the check is about structure, not keyword matching.
Update the READMEs that currently fail rather than loosening the check.

title: test: assert no workflow uses a mutable action reference
description: A test that fails when any workflow references an action by tag or branch instead of a commit SHA.
why: Pinning actions by SHA is the repository's policy and it is currently maintained by hand, which is why two references are still on a tag. A mutable reference lets someone else change what runs in CI, and policies kept by review rather than by test do not stay complete.
criteria: Every `uses:` reference is checked for a 40-character SHA.
A tag or branch reference fails with the workflow and line named.
Local and reusable-workflow references are handled correctly rather than reported as violations.
A version comment is required alongside the SHA.
guidance: `internal/doccheck/workflows_test.go` already parses the workflows — extend it rather than adding another parser.
Local `./.github/...` references have no SHA and must not be flagged.
Requiring the trailing version comment keeps the pins readable.

title: test: assert every public make target appears in make help
description: A test that compares `.PHONY` targets against the `help` output and fails on a target missing from either.
why: The Makefile is the documented entry point for every check, and `help` is how contributors find them. Targets have been added without a help line before — the `.PHONY` list and the help text are maintained separately, so they drift silently and the newest targets are the least discoverable.
criteria: Every public `.PHONY` target has a help line.
A help line for a target that no longer exists fails the test.
Internal targets can be excluded by a documented convention.
The test runs as part of `go test ./...`.
guidance: Parse the Makefile rather than hard-coding the target list.
Pick an explicit convention for internal targets instead of inferring from naming.
`internal/doccheck` is the natural home, beside the other consistency checks.

title: feat(api): String method for CredentialArm
description: A `String` method on `CredentialArm` returning its stable identifier, matching the values `Inspect` reports.
why: `CredentialArm` is a string type with four constants, and the report types already have `String` methods. Formatting an arm with `%v` works by accident today, so any future change to the underlying type would silently change log and report output.
criteria: `String` returns the same identifiers `EntryInfo.CredentialType` uses.
An unknown arm returns a clearly-marked unknown value rather than an empty string.
A test asserts the method and the inspect report cannot disagree.
The method is documented as stable, since consumers match on it.
guidance: Derive the identifiers from `inspect.go` so the two cannot drift.
An empty string for an unknown value is the trap; return something recognisable instead.
Follow the existing `String` methods' style on the report types.

title: feat(api): typed constants for the authorized function types
description: Exported constants for the three authorized function types, mirroring how the credential arms are exposed.
why: The arms are exported as a typed vocabulary, but a caller branching on the function type has to reach into the SDK's generated enum, whose names are doubled and awkward. The repository already decided this vocabulary belongs in its own types; the function types were simply not included.
criteria: All three types have constants, named consistently with the arm constants.
Conversion to and from the SDK's enum is provided and tested round-trip.
An unrecognised value produces the existing unsupported-function-type error rather than a zero value.
A test fails if the SDK gains a function type with no constant here.
guidance: Enumerate from the SDK's `xdr` package and cite the file.
The completeness test is what keeps this current as the protocol grows.
Fail closed on unknown values; the sentinel error for that already exists.

title: feat(api): report whether an entry is fully signed
description: A helper answering whether every node of an entry that needs a signature has one.
why: `Inspect` reports a `Signed` flag per node and the documentation tells callers to walk the tree themselves. Everyone writes that walk, it is easy to get wrong on a nested delegates tree, and a wrong answer means submitting an entry that fails on chain after fees.
criteria: Every node at every depth is considered, including nested delegates.
A source-account entry is reported as not requiring a signature rather than as unsigned.
An empty `ScvVec` counts as unsigned, consistent with `Inspect`.
Tests cover each arm, including a partially-signed delegate tree.
guidance: Reuse `Inspect`'s report rather than re-walking the XDR, so the two cannot disagree.
The source-account case is the one that makes a naive version wrong.
Match `Inspect`'s existing definition of signed exactly, including the empty-vector rule.

title: feat(api): expose the library version
description: An exported constant or function giving the library's version, used by the CLI's `--version` rather than only a build-time variable.
why: The CLI reports a version stamped by the linker, so a consumer importing the library as a package has no way to report which version they are on. Bug reports then arrive without a version, and the bindings have no version to pass across the FFI either.
criteria: The version is readable from Go code with no build-time flags.
The CLI's `--version` and the library value cannot disagree, asserted by a test.
The release process updates it, and a check fails if a tag and the constant diverge.
The bindings can report it.
guidance: A test tying the constant to the tag is what prevents the usual stale-constant problem.
The CLI already has `main.version` stamped — reconcile rather than adding a second notion of version.
The C ABI's version symbol work is related; keep the two consistent.

title: feat(integrations): the service's health endpoint reports its version
description: Include the library and build version in the health response.
why: Diagnosing a deployed service starts with which version is running, and the health endpoint does not say. Operators resort to checking the image tag, which is the deployment's intent rather than what is actually running — and those differ exactly when something has gone wrong.
criteria: The health response includes the library version and the build commit.
The OpenAPI specification is updated and the drift check passes.
No configuration, secret or environment detail is exposed alongside it.
A test asserts the fields are present and non-empty.
guidance: Version information is fine to expose; configuration is not — keep the response minimal.
The specification drift check will fail if the schema is not updated with it.
Reuse the library version work rather than adding another build-time variable.

title: feat(integrations): the GitHub Action reports the version it used
description: Include the soroauth version in the action's output and job summary.
why: The action's verdict is evidence a reviewer relies on, and evidence without a version cannot be reproduced later. When the analyzer's findings change between versions, a summary in an old pull request becomes unattributable.
criteria: The version appears in the job summary and as an action output.
It identifies the exact build, not just a tag.
A test asserts the version appears in the summary.
The documentation shows how to pin the action for reproducible results.
guidance: Report the build identity rather than the action's own ref; those can differ.
Reuse the library version work instead of adding a second source.
The README should say how to pin, since reproducibility is the point.
